title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.

title: A Sneak Peek on the Dark Side: First DarkSide-20k Analysis Workshop
location: The University of Chicago John W. Boyer Center in Paris
description:
A wide range of astrophysical and cosmological measurements indicates that the universe is filled with far more matter than what we can account for by looking around us. This excess matter is called dark matter and, while it is thought to be constituted by a new, exotic species of elementary particle, its nature remains unknown — making it one of the biggest puzzles in modern particle physics and cosmology.
 DarkSide-20k (DS-20k) is an experiment currently under construction at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso, beneath the Apennine Mountains in Italy. It aims to detect the potential feeble interactions of dark matter particles using an innovative detector featuring a 50-tonne target of specially sourced argon, extracted from underground gas reservoirs in Colorado and depleted in the radioactive isotopes that typically contaminate argon extracted from air. This massive, low-background target, instrumented as a two-phase Time Projection Chamber, is expected to feature a sensitivity to dark matter exceeding that of any currently running experiment.
 The event, held at the University of Chicago’s John W. Boyer Center in Paris, is the first collaboration-wide analysis workshop — previous workshops were much smaller in scale — and aims to kickstart the finalization of the study of DS-20k’s sensitivity to dark matter. By the end of the workshop, the organizers aims to be able to run the full simulation and analysis pipeline, evaluating the final sensitivity of the experiment while accounting for the finer details of the detector response. The workshop will also train a new cohort of researchers to become core members of the analysis team in preparation to early data. The event is organized by the International Institute of Research in Paris, with primary support from The University of Chicago and the Université Paris Cité, and with the participation of AstroCeNT.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

title: Sociology Colloquium with Sanyu A. Mojola, our Distinguished Alumni Lecture
location: Social Science Research, Room 305 (Albion Small Room)
description:
“Death by Design: Producing Racial Health Inequality in the Shadow of the Capitol “
 Talk Abstract:
 Washington, DC, the capital of the United States, has the nation’s largest racial life expectancy gap, and it has experienced many of the nation’s worst epidemics, including maternal and infant mortality, homicide, heroin overdoses, and HIV/AIDS. These epidemics have disproportionately affected African Americans. Why and how does racial health inequality exist and persist? Starting from the city’s founding in the late 1700s until 2022, and drawing on a range of sources—including archival material, life history interviews, and census, vital statistics, and disease surveillance data—the talk will illustrate how the physical, social, and policy design of the city contributes to the production and reproduction of disproportionate Black death. 
 Biography: Sanyu A. Mojola is Professor of Sociology and Public Affairs and the Maurice P. During Professor of Demographic Studies at Princeton University. She directed Princeton’s Office of Population Research between 2020 – 2024. She earned her Ph.D in Sociology from the University of Chicago in 2008. Her mixed methods research examines how societies produce health and illness in various settings such as Kenya, South Africa and the United States. She has investigated how social dynamics within schools, communities, labor markets, cities and eco-systems can lead to health inequality. She is especially interested in how the life course, gender, race/ethnicity and socio-economic status shape health outcomes. Her publications include two books with University of California Press: Love, Money and HIV: Becoming a Modern African Woman in the Age of AIDS (2014) and Death by Design: Producing Racial Health Inequality in the Shadow of the Capitol (2025) as well as journal articles in outlets such as the American Journal of Sociology, Population and Development Review, Demography, Gender and Society, Social Science and Medicine and the American Journal of Public Health, among other outlets. She is currently working on her third book, tentatively titled “Nowadays Diseases: Aging through Social Change in Rural Post-Apartheid South Africa.” Additionally, her NIH-funded research group is investigating various aspects of the geography of health in the United States. She is currently serving as deputy editor at the American Sociological Review and editorial committee member at Population and Development Review. Please see her webpages for more information: https://sociology.princeton.edu/people/sanyu-mojola and https://scholar.princeton.edu/smojola.

title: Guided Tour of the Newberry
description:
In 1893, the World’s Columbian Exposition took place in Chicago, Grover Cleveland started his second non-consecutive term as president, and the Newberry building opened to the public. On this guided tour, you’ll learn about the history behind the founding of the Newberry. You’ll also discover all the ways you can engage with the library today.
Founded in 1887, the Newberry had three temporary locations before moving into its permanent home across from Washington Square Park in 1893.
The library was designed by architect Henry Ives Cobb, with input from Newberry head librarian William Frederick Poole. Cobb envisioned a grand edifice on par with the civic landmarks of Europe; Poole favored a more modest design that would facilitate user access to books and other resources. In the end, they compromised. The Newberry is a blend of their competing visions.
Aerial photograph of the Newberry, 2022
Architectural detail on the Newberry's facade
A quiet study space on the Newberry's third floor
Over the years, the Newberry has grown and evolved, notably with the addition of a climate-controlled stacks building in the early 1980s and a renovation that updated spaces and restored original architectural details on the library’s first floor in 2018.
You’ll get a healthy dose of history on this tour. But you’ll also get to see the Newberry in action in the present. Tens of thousands of people visit the Newberry every year, and there are many ways that we make the library’s collections, programs, and resources accessible and relevant to them.
This tour is free, and no advance registration is required. We'll meet in the lobby of the Newberry and begin the tour from there.

title: Raise the Red Lantern
description:
DIRECTED BY
Yimou Zhang
WRITTEN BY
Tong Su,
Ni Zhen
STARRING
Gong Li,
Jingwu Ma,
Saifei He
Nineteen-year-old Songlian, a promising student whose family has been destroyed by her father's death, is forced to abandon her studies and marry into wealth, becoming the fourth and newest concubine of the aging, unseen Master Chen. Inside his walled estate, she discovers a household ruled by a merciless ritual: each night, red lanterns are lit outside the chambers of whichever wife the master chooses to visit, granting her privilege and status while the others are cast into cold irrelevance. Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul.
“As visually striking as it is dramatically effective,” Zhang Yimou’s Academy Award-nominated Raise the Red Lantern sumptuously captures 1920s China while “subtly exploring the politics of power and control” (Janet Maslin, The New York Times). One of international cinema’s greatest stars of the era, Gong Li is “nuanced and understated” (Chicago Reader) as the stifled young woman forced into a repressive world of concubinage. Newly restored, the film stands as one of the defining works of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and international film of the 1990s.
The 4K restoration of Raise the Red Lantern was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong - Bologna).

title: Commemoration of World AIDS Day Ft. the Work of Niki de Saint Phalle
description:
The significance of World AIDS Day lies in both remembrance and community. Each year at Wrightwood 659, we honor those lost to AIDS while creating a space for family, friends, and loved ones to come together in celebration of their lives.
Join us on December 2 for a special program featuring Niki de Saint Phalle's influential illustrated book AIDS: You can't catch it holding hands (1986). Saint Phalle—whose work is featured in our current exhibition Inner Worlds—created the book for her son, Philip, as a compassionate and accessible introduction to the realities of AIDS. Through vivid illustrations and direct storytelling, she challenged the fear and misinformation surrounding the disease, emphasizing the importance of empathy, understanding, and human connection.
Reflecting Wrightwood 659’s long-standing commitment to artists whose lives and work have been shaped by the HIV/AIDS epidemic, the evening will also include a tribute to John Peller, who is stepping down as President and CEO of AIDS Foundation Chicago after more than a decade of leadership. Since joining the organization in 2005 and becoming CEO in 2014, Peller has helped advance HIV prevention, treatment, housing, and health-equity initiatives across Chicago and beyond.

title: Be A Part of A Film: America Ever After with Eboo Patel
description:
Come be part of a movie! (And have some Chipotle and Insomnia Cookies on us)
 The Nantucket Project presents:
 America Ever After
 A presentation from renowned social entrepreneur Eboo Patel, recorded for a film in production
 RSVP Required, filming 12/2 and 12/3 6-7:30pm, Logan Center Theater West
 What it’s All About…
 Every day, America wakes up and tells itself a bad story: one of
 irreconcilable differences, of our inability to live together
 productively. This doom-and-gloom narrative has seeped so deeply into
 our consciousness that it seems to have become a self-fulfilling
 prophecy.
 There is a better story to tell.
 In America Ever After, Eboo Patel shows that the American story is the
 triumph of pluralism over the multi-headed monster of separatism,
 bigotry and intransigent identity politics. Eboo shows that
 the core conflict animating American history is how we balance our two
 selves: the self we inherited from our grandparents and the self we
 share in our identity as Americans. If we retreat too far into the
 tribe of our grandparents, we risk separatism—whether it is the ‘blood
 and soil’ camp on the right or those on the left who argue we have
 never been equal and therefore reject the possibility of unity.
 And yet, if we lean too far in the other direction, we risk
 assimilation: the erasure of differences in the name of a common
 identity. Drawing inspiration from a cast of renegades, patriots and
 unlikely heroes—some familiar, others less so—Eboo reanimates the
 story of America.
 It is the triumph of the inalienable right to be different. And for
 your neighbor to be different, too.
 If this is a story that people today feel detached from, or feel is
 out of reach, Eboo shows us that our nation’s greatest heroes grappled
 with challenges remarkably like our own today. Spoiler alert: it’s the
 greatest success story in the history of the world.
 Participants understand that this event is being filmed to be part of an upcoming documentary and by attending they consent to be filmed and potentially to be included in the documentary.
 To learn more about the Nantucket Project visit https://nantucketproject.com/

Douglas Tirola’s thrilling documentary portrait of famed composer and conductor Leonard Bernstein artistically tells the story of an immigrant son who became a phenomenon as the visionary and exuberant conductor of the New York Philharmonic, and, then for decades, the face of classical music for the nation. Bernstein joyfully responded to the clamor of his times, matching his passion for music with an unyielding commitment to political engagement. Tirola also reveals a husband and father wrestling with what Bernstein called "his demons" of his hidden sexuality. We see Bernstein as a tireless participant in the anti-war and civil rights movements and a factor in the de-escalation of tensions between the U.S. and U.S.S.R. Incredibly Tirola uses Bernstein’s own voice almost exclusively to turn the maestro's life story into a call to action for artists and those that believe in the arts to create change in today's society with the goal of bringing freedom and respect to all people.
BERNSTEIN’S WALL is a cinematic portrait of legendary conductor and composer Leonard Bernstein. Told in Bernstein’s own words through never-before-seen archival footage, Director Douglas Tirola explores Bernstein’s art, activism, politics, family, and sexuality, while asking the question: “Can the artist still create change?”

title: ISAC Lecture with Dr. Maggie Geoga
location: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC), Breasted Hall
description:
The Power of Poetry in Ancient Egypt
 This talk explores conceptions of poetic writing in ancient Egypt, from ideas of what literature was and what it meant to its readers, to experiments with what poetic language could and couldn’t do, to questions of how poetry signifies. Through examinations of several ancient Egyptian poems—including as The Words of Khakheperreseneb, with its startlingly modern discussion of the difficulty of originality, and The Eloquent Peasant, with its pessimistic irony—the talk reveals an ambivalence among ancient writers about the value of poetic language and what it could achieve, as well as identifies new paths forward in the study of ancient Egyptian literature.
 Margaret Geoga’s research combines Egyptology and literary studies to focus on ancient Egyptian literature, its interpretation by ancient and modern readers alike, and the reception history of ancient Egypt in later periods. Her other research interests include scribal culture, Middle and Late Egyptian, book history, history of Egyptology, translation studies, and literary theory.Maggie’s first book focuses on The Teaching of Amenemhat, an enigmatic and unusually popular ancient Egyptian poem that unusually depicts the murder of a king. The monograph investigates the poem’s transmission and reception by its numerous ancient readers, closely examining a selection of the poem’s approximately 250 surviving manuscripts in order to explore how readers interpreted and reinterpreted this text over the course of 1000 years in both Egypt and Nubia.Maggie earned her PhD in Egyptology from Brown University, where she also completed a concurrent MA in Comparative Literature. Her work has been supported by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, the Fritz Thyssen Foundation, the American Philosophical Society, and the McKeon Center at the University of Chicago. Maggie has previously been an Andrew W. Mellon Postdoctoral Fellow in the Humanities at the Wolf Humanities Center of the University of Pennsylvania, a Junior Fellow in the Society of Fellows in Critical Bibliography, and the Terrace Research Associate in Egyptian Art at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

title: Aelita: Queen of Mars
description:
Before science fiction conquered Hollywood, Soviet filmmakers were already dreaming about life on Mars.
Yakov Protazanov’s 1924 Aelita: Queen of Mars is one of the landmarks of early science-fiction cinema—a wildly imaginative mixture of romance, revolution, social satire, and interplanetary fantasy.
The story moves between the upheaval of post-revolutionary Moscow and an astonishing vision of Mars ruled by the beautiful Queen Aelita. The film’s extraordinary Constructivist sets and costumes remain some of the most striking images of the silent era, creating a futuristic world unlike almost anything that came before it.
For Score & Screen, this groundbreaking film is reimagined with a new original score performed live at The CheckOut, bringing a contemporary musical voice to a century-old vision of the future.

New additions to the cast include aerialist Melissa James, hand-to-hand acrobatic specialists Jack and Anna, and Iris Ileven who specializes in hand balance and contortion:

 Noone, a four-time American Ninja Warrior competitor and Guinness World Record holder, is ecstatic to return to the national tour of A Magical Cirque Christmas. She is known for her versatile performances and her role in the contemporary circus company Cirque Vida, based in Austin, TX.
 Las Vegas resident Stoinev is a fifth-generation circus performer who started juggling at the age of five and hasn’t stopped ever since. At eight years old, he was invited to perform at Premier Rampe, an International Circus Festival hosted in Monaco.
 James combines musical theatre, dance, and circus into one dynamic performance. A former Dance Captain for Chicago, Hairspray, and Mamma Mia, she later collaborated with legendary director Franco Dragone as both an artist and creative. Having headlined productions across the Middle East, the U.K., Asia, Australia, and the U.S., James brings a global perspective and cinematic storytelling to every performance.
 Jack and Anna perform hand-to-hand acrobatics, combining elite athleticism with trust, precision, and artistry. Jack is a former Canadian National Champion in Senior Elite Men’s Pair with more than 15 years of experience as a base, while Anna graduated from l’École de Cirque de Québec with a concentration in hand-to-hand acrobatics.
 Ileven is a Las Vegas-based hand balancer and contortionist, who performs elegant, emotionally driven acts that have captivated audiences and blend strength, flexibility, and expressive artistry.
Audience members across the country have praised A Magical Cirque Christmas as a must-see holiday tradition. “Absolutely fantastic show. We took our six- and three-year-olds and all had the best time,” said one reviewer. “We will be making this a yearly Christmas tradition!” Another audience member called it “great for the whole family,” adding,“The cast is incredibly talented. Mark keeps everyone laughing between the exciting acts.” Fans consistently praise the show’s world-class performers, breathtaking acrobatics, festive atmosphere and family-friendly entertainment.
Attendees of all ages at A Magical Cirque Christmas will delight in the graceful, flexible, and hypnotic acrobatics, stunning gravity-defying performances and high-flying aerial artists, as well as many more surprises.

Giulio Brouzet is a chromatic harmonica player living in Chicago. His music blends Chicago blues with influences from New Orleans, Cajun, Americana, folk, and early jazz. Using chromatic, diatonic, bass, and custom-tuned harmonicas—plus guitar, kazoo, nose flute, and foot percussion—he reinterprets songs by Jimmy Reed, Sonny Boy Williamson, Walter Horton, Louis Armstrong, Hank Williams, and Gershwin.
Originally from Italy, Giulio grew up surrounded by his parents’ record collection and chose the harmonica as his lifelong companion. For over three decades, he has performed across Europe and the U.S. in clubs, theaters, churches, and festivals, with jazz orchestras, blues bands, and solo. His work spans performance, improvisation, ethnomusicology, and music therapy.

description:
Two 
calibers of singers exist in today’s music industry. There are vocalists and 
then there are entertainers. Laretha Weathersby is both. Her dynamic, effervescent stage presence 
is unparalleled and her sultry, wispy vibrato makes her a Blues natural.
Voted 
2009-2010’s “Chicago Blues Diva of the Year,” she belts out traditional Blues 
classics with passion and poise and delivers riveting renditions of timeless 
R&B, Soul and Top 40 tunes, all while captivating crowds with her jovial 
disposition and dynamic dancing. Known for her rousing stage presence, crowd members rarely 
blink when Laretha hits the stage, fearing they will miss one of her signature 
dance moves or the chance to chant along with the charismatic chanteuse.
Reigning 
from the Southside of Chicago, Laretha’s mother, a former Gospel soloist, 
detected her daughter’s singing abilities and enrolled the toddler in piano classes 
and encouraged her as a teenager to be an active member of the choir at the 
family’s place of worship. But it was not until the 1990s that Laretha began to 
cultivate a personal relationship with Blues music.
Emerging 
as one of the premiere female Blues vocalists in the City of Chicago in the 
late 1990s, Laretha has performed at such legendary Blues hotspots as The 
Kingston Mines, BLUES on Halsted and since 2010 is a spectacular presence here 
at BLUE CHICAGO.
Her 
debut album – Dance the Blues Away – is an eclectic mix of traditional Blues 
infused with remnants of contemporary R&B and Soul. The album reveals 
Laretha’s reverence for conventional Blues music while flaunting her fluent 
transition into contemporary R & B and Soul.
According 
to Ms. Weathersby, “the power of Blues music lies in its ability to relate to 
each and every member of the human race. People of all different backgrounds 
can connect with the universal concepts of love, triumph and tribulation, which 
are the very elements upon which Blues music is based. I consider it an honor 
and joy to incorporate that human element into my live performances and it is 
with passion and humility that I accept the honor and challenge of preserving 
Blues music for future generations.”

title: Richie Pardo The Late Set
description:
Richie Pardo began his career as a pianist in R&B bands and Chicago jazz groups before making the move to bass in 1979. He has since been a fixture in the Chicago jazz community, leading quartets and quintets, and collaborating with notable musicians such as Todd Herbert, Art Davis, Tim Davis, and Kevin O’Connell. His style blends solid, melodic bass lines with inventive, exploratory solos, influenced in part by the legacy of Oscar Pettiford.
Pardo’s work is marked by a “clearly delineated bass” that both anchors the rhythm and ventures into melodic exploration. His 2010 album I Get the Message, Volume 1: The Genius of Oscar Pettiford is a tribute to Pettiford, featuring collaborations with violinist Mark Feldman, tenorist Ron Dewar, pianist Jeremy Kahn, and drummer Bill “Bugs” Cochran.
Pardo is never slavish in his homages to his hero; rather, he puts his own contemporary stamp on the material throughout. Nor does he leave any doubt that he’s a take-charge kind of guy; not content for a minute to play a supporting role, he’s a smart enough leader to know what he’s got in these musicians and to allow them their own say in these lovingly rendered interpretations.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago

title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.

title: ISAC Exhibit: Hartapu: The Forgotten King of Anatolia
location: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC) Museum
description:
Seven years ago, Hartapu was little more than a name. Then, in 2019, an inscribed stone pulled from an irrigation canal in central Türkiye introduced the world to a king who claimed to have conquered Phrygia—one of the most powerful kingdoms of the ancient world. Suddenly, a ruler and a kingdom largely unknown to history demanded a place on the map of Iron Age Anatolia. The stone was found at Türkmen-Karahöyük, a massive tell rising 35 meters above the Konya Plain, that must have been Hartapu’s capital. Though the site had gone largely unnoticed by archaeologists, it is one of the largest Iron Age sites in Anatolia—and excavations launched in 2024 by ISAC and Bilkent University (Ankara, Türkiye) are only beginning to reveal the city’s historical development.
 Hartapu ruled in the eighth century BCE, during a period of intense rivalry between great powers—Phrygia to the west, the Neo-Assyrian Empire to the east—and his kingdom sat squarely between them. The exhibition tells his story through ancient inscriptions, archaeological finds, and new technologies, including 3D printing and advanced imaging, that are transforming how scholars study the past. Contemporary works by artist SaraNoa Mark offer a counterpoint, reflecting on landscape, memory, and the labor and care of preserving the past.
 The ISAC Museum special exhibition Hartapu: The Forgotten King of Anatolia is on view from September 17, 2026 through March 14, 2027. It is accessible with museum admission during museum hours.

title: A Sneak Peek on the Dark Side: First DarkSide-20k Analysis Workshop
location: The University of Chicago John W. Boyer Center in Paris
description:
A wide range of astrophysical and cosmological measurements indicates that the universe is filled with far more matter than what we can account for by looking around us. This excess matter is called dark matter and, while it is thought to be constituted by a new, exotic species of elementary particle, its nature remains unknown — making it one of the biggest puzzles in modern particle physics and cosmology.
 DarkSide-20k (DS-20k) is an experiment currently under construction at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso, beneath the Apennine Mountains in Italy. It aims to detect the potential feeble interactions of dark matter particles using an innovative detector featuring a 50-tonne target of specially sourced argon, extracted from underground gas reservoirs in Colorado and depleted in the radioactive isotopes that typically contaminate argon extracted from air. This massive, low-background target, instrumented as a two-phase Time Projection Chamber, is expected to feature a sensitivity to dark matter exceeding that of any currently running experiment.
 The event, held at the University of Chicago’s John W. Boyer Center in Paris, is the first collaboration-wide analysis workshop — previous workshops were much smaller in scale — and aims to kickstart the finalization of the study of DS-20k’s sensitivity to dark matter. By the end of the workshop, the organizers aims to be able to run the full simulation and analysis pipeline, evaluating the final sensitivity of the experiment while accounting for the finer details of the detector response. The workshop will also train a new cohort of researchers to become core members of the analysis team in preparation to early data. The event is organized by the International Institute of Research in Paris, with primary support from The University of Chicago and the Université Paris Cité, and with the participation of AstroCeNT.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

title: Lera Malchenko: If Violence is Granular Enough
location: Franke Institute for the Humanities Regenstein Library, Room S-102
description:
About the Talk: Russia rolled out its digital occupation of Ukraine almost simultaneously with its kinetic operations. Using OSINT methods, Lera Malchenko collected evidence of how the occupation’s digital infrastructure was deployed in the occupied territories, and of the companies and developers who build and run it. The talk shows how extrastatecraft becomes more effective once it adopts classic IT development approaches, from startup structures and sprints to hackathons, and revisits Zygmunt Bauman’s concept of “bureaucrats of violence” in the context of contemporary digital occupation. 
 About the Project: The talk is based on Lera’s essay “If Violence is Granular Enough,” written for Occupational Formations: Infrastructures of the Seen and Unseen. The group emerged in 2025 as a grassroots project supported by Documenting Ukraine, a program of the Institute for Human Sciences (IWM Vienna). Its interdisciplinary team of researchers, writers, artists, educators, filmmakers, and analysts examines the infrastructures Russia is deploying in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, from tactics of erasure to the militarization of existing systems and the building of new ones, both seen and unseen, with a particular interest in what escapes the gaze and mainstream media narratives.
 Lera Malchenko is an investigative researcher, interdisciplinary artist, and filmmaker. She is a co-founder of the art collective “fantastic little splash” and an independent research project “Occupational Formations”.
 This event is free and open to the public and is sponsored by the Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures, with the gracious support of the Otto V. Čapek Fund. If you enjoy this type of programming, please feel free to join us for the City to City: Dnipro Meets Chicago symposium on December 4-5.

title: Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? Gallery Hours
description:
Arts + Public Life at the University of Chicago presents Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? a new exhibition by Chicago artist Candace Hunter centered on the construction of the Dan Ryan Expressway and the Black communities displaced in its path. Now embedded within Chicago’s physical and social fabric, the Dan Ryan Expressway obscures both the choices that produced it and the lives reorganized around it. The construction disrupted the ordinary intimacies through which a place becomes home: routes traveled, neighbors known, businesses frequented, porches gathered on.
 Through photographic collage, architectural fragments, archival materials, sound, sculptural interventions, and oral histories, Hunter moves between what is documented and what is remembered. The work resists the idea that displacement can be understood solely through statistics.
 The series builds on the Memory Teas Candace hosted during her APL residency, which gathered first-person accounts from Black Chicagoans who remember the Dan Ryan’s construction and the neighborhoods transformed by it. Rather than asking these memories to complete the historical record, Hunter allows them to stay partial, layered, and unresolved.
 While centered on Chicago’s South Side, the history at the heart of Intentionality, 1960 reaches beyond the city. Across the United States, highway construction, redevelopment, and urban renewal reshaped Black communities, often presenting profound social and spatial disruption as necessary progress. Intentionality, 1960 invites audiences to see those histories not as isolated events but as part of a larger American story.
 Intentionality, 1960 will be accompanied by Threshold: Conversations on the Stoop, a series of public dialogues on the front porch within the exhibition between Candace and scholars to dive into topics related to the exhibition. The Threshold conversations are presented with support from the Office of the Provost Diversity and Inclusion team, in partnership with the Chicago Forum for Free Inquiry and Expression.
 Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? will be on view from September 24-December 12 in the Arts + Public Life Gallery Space located in the Arts Incubator at 301 E. Garfield Blvd.
 Gallery Hours: Thursday-Saturday | 1:00 - 5:00pm

title: Raise the Red Lantern
description:
DIRECTED BY
Yimou Zhang
WRITTEN BY
Tong Su,
Ni Zhen
STARRING
Gong Li,
Jingwu Ma,
Saifei He
Nineteen-year-old Songlian, a promising student whose family has been destroyed by her father's death, is forced to abandon her studies and marry into wealth, becoming the fourth and newest concubine of the aging, unseen Master Chen. Inside his walled estate, she discovers a household ruled by a merciless ritual: each night, red lanterns are lit outside the chambers of whichever wife the master chooses to visit, granting her privilege and status while the others are cast into cold irrelevance. Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul.
“As visually striking as it is dramatically effective,” Zhang Yimou’s Academy Award-nominated Raise the Red Lantern sumptuously captures 1920s China while “subtly exploring the politics of power and control” (Janet Maslin, The New York Times). One of international cinema’s greatest stars of the era, Gong Li is “nuanced and understated” (Chicago Reader) as the stifled young woman forced into a repressive world of concubinage. Newly restored, the film stands as one of the defining works of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and international film of the 1990s.
The 4K restoration of Raise the Red Lantern was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong - Bologna).

title: RDI Workshop Series - Michelle Nancy Huang
description:
Join RDI on Thursday, December 3, from 4:00-5:30 pm in Kelly 108, for the RDI Workshop Series with Professor Michelle Nancy Huang
 This workshop is based on the introduction to Huang’s first book, Racial Beings: Contemporary Experiments in New Materialisms (ANIMA series, Duke, March 2026). In Racial Beings, Huang brings a feminist new materialist lens to bear on contemporary Asian American literature’s innovative play with discourses of science and technology. She argues that emerging from these works are “molecular aesthetics”—formal experiments that diminish the boundaries of the human—that challenge the lay perception of racial identity as a trait of an individual human. Instead, molecular aesthetics reveal how race permeates the matter of the world. Reading works by authors such as Ruth Ozeki, Larissa Lai, Mei-mei Berssenbrugge, and Julie Otsuka through scientific discourses like quantum physics, genetic engineering, and elemental chemistry, Huang develops a synthetic reading practice that shows 1) the nexus of race and science is not reducible to scientific racism, and 2) science can provide an unlikely creative reservoir for Asian American writers and artists that allows us to imagine alternative ways of understanding racial being beyond the limits of the human individual.​​​​​​​
 Michelle N. Huang is Associate Professor of English and Asian American Studies at Northwestern University. Her first book, Racial Beings: Experiments in Asian American New Materialisms (Duke University Press, 2026) examines posthumanist aesthetics in post-1965 Asian American literature to trace racial representation beyond the individual human character. Her work appears in Journal of Asian American Studies, American Literature, Contemporary Literature, and American Quarterly, among other venues. Currently, Michelle is president of the Association for the Study of Arts of the Present (ASAP), editing a special issue on periodization for Post45, and at work on her second book project on Asian American literature and biomedicine. Her film essay, INHUMAN FIGURES: Robots, Clones, and Aliens, can be viewed online at the Smithsonian Asian Pacific American Center website. ​​​​​​​
 A pre-circulated paper will be made available the Friday before the workshop for those who RSVP.

title: Grace Lavery on Personal Demons with Jonathan Flatley
description:
Please join the us for a conversation with Grace Lavery (Professor English, UC Berkeley) and Jonathan Flatley (Professor English, UChicago) over Grace’s recent monograph, Personal Demons: Possession Narratives of Late Liberalism (Duke University Press, 2026).
 Personal Demons offers a new theory of the relation between sex, desire, and personhood, asking what we should make of the many contemporary instances when bodies seem to want different things from the consciousnesses within them. Grace Lavery maps the negative energies—demonic, incoherent, resistant—through which liberalism produces and disciplines its scapegoats. Through an examination of modern possession narratives, from racialized spectacles of bodily transformation and disguise to the liturgy of the Church of Scientology, Lavery unspools the knot of body, affect, and representation at the end of liberalism. In the face of the uneasy bargains queer and trans liberal organizations made with the phobic state, Personal Demons elaborates a vision of queer collective living that does not assume a shared concept of interiority, taking the incompatibility of such concepts as the founding axiom for a coalition against the ideological regulation of bodies and minds.

LADY RADIATOR
Lady Radiator is a New Jersey-born two-piece band built on intensity and resilience. Formed in 2007 by Kenny Collette and Adam Kobylarz, the band quickly made waves signing with Emerald Moon Records, touring nationwide, and sharing stages with The Sleeping, Portugal The Man, and Mayday Parade. Now, fueled by a viral resurgence on TikTok and in partnership with Interscope Records , the band has returned with a fire that’s louder, sharper, and hungrier than ever. The Lady Radiator movement has begun.
HELEN 55
Helen 55 formed in the vibrant North Hollywood Arts District of California in 1997.
Their debut release, a 3-song cassette tape featuring the track “Dumb Summer,” quickly gained traction through internet trading, earning them a global following. They began performing at iconic venues such as The Whisky a Go-Go and The Roxy Theatre, sharing stages with notable bands like System of a Down, Papa Roach, and Alien Ant Farm.
In January 2000, the group self-released their debut CD, “Amped.” Their rising profile was boosted by a feature on MTV’s “Snowed In Undercover” and an interview with Matt Pinfield for Farmclub TV, establishing them as a “buzz band”.
Despite growing recognition, the band disbanded in 2002. They reunited in 2010 and have since released two albums: 2010’s “Helen 55” and 2021’s “SLEEP | DEATH” (pronounced “The Fine Line Between Sleep and Death”).
UPON YOUR DEAD BODY
Upon Your Dead Body consists of Efrain Benavides, Robert De La Rosa on drums and Jesus Trevino on bass, the band’s sound is a fusion of spoken word, melodic intensity, midwest emo, and math rock. Together, they deliver raw emotion and a captivating edge that has been making waves across Texas. Drawing inspiration from acts like La Dispute, Coheed and Cambria, Hail The Sun, and Mom Jeans. title: 1st Set With Mario Abney
description:
As a Chicago native, Mario Abney’s trumpet playing fuses traditional and extended techniques in an inventive way. His uniquely personal vision for music endows it with an infinite array of tonal colors. He is recognized for his ability to create pure musical dialogues and hear music in a universally spiritual way. These qualities make him one of New Orleans’ most pioneering young jazz musicians.
Trumpeter, composer and bandleader Mario Abney’s musical career began at age 7 when he was introduced to the piano by his uncle Arthur. Influenced by both his uncle’s playing and the musical background of his church, Abney developed a love and fascination for music that grew throughout his years in high school. It was during this time that his interest turned from piano and drums to wind instruments; however, he continued to hone his percussion skills by playing drums for church services.
Mario’s first encounter with jazz was when he heard the sounds of trumpeter Wynton Marsalis. This sparked a fascination and soon Mario began to explore music by Louis Armstrong, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis and other great trumpet players who established this genre.
Fast forwarding to 2024, Mario Abney is once again gracing the stages of his beloved hometown Chicago. From iconic venues to up-and-coming spots, he’s become a regular feature with fans eagerly anticipating each and every performance.

description:

What happens to the ideal of meritocracy when success depends partly on the background we inherit and the identities we develop?  Join the Markets & Society Committee for an off-the-record dinner discussion with Derek Neal, the William C. Norby Professor of Economics in the Kenneth C. Griffin Department of Economics at the University of Chicago. Neal’s research examines how criminal justice policies affect racial inequality and how incentive and accountability systems are designed for U.S. educators. Together, we’ll explore the relationship between culture, economic opportunity, and the institutions that shape wealth outcomes.

title: Sam and Joe Eichner, "Our Greatest Work"
description:
About the Book:
Our Greatest Work opens with a panic attack, a celebrity cameo, and an antique gun: Joe, an actor, is traveling from Paris to Chicago for his ten-year high school reunion, where he plans to confront his twin brother Sam, a writer.
In alternating chapters from each twin’s point of view—Joe writing as Joe, Sam as Sam—we learn of the slights that started, then prolonged, their confounding estrangement. There’s the fateful high school production of Rent. An illicit affair set to Death Cab for Cutie. A pathetic act of violence in a Florentine study abroad apartment. All the while, a mysterious (if idiotic) childhood friend is pulling strings from behind the scenes, his motivations troublingly obscure . . .
As the reunion draws near, a tragicomic series of events conspire to bring the brothers’ artistic and romantic entanglements to the fore. In a Parent Trap-esque twist, Joe and Sam switch places, albeit to less-than heartwarming results. When our protagonists finally collide at the reunion on the banks of Lake Michigan, they’re forced to answer an inevitable question: Can either of us truly live while the other is still alive?
Inspired as much by Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan Quartet as ’90s sex comedies, the Eichners’ novel is at once a moving portrait of brotherhood, an antic satire of the entertainment industry, and a profound exploration of what it means to be an original when your very existence threatens to make you redundant.
About the Authors:
SAM EICHNER is a writer from the Chicagoland area. His work has appeared in Cleveland Review of Books, Joyland Magazine, Columbia Journalism Review, and Bloomberg, among other outlets. He currently lives in Brooklyn with his wife and cat.
JOE EICHNER earned his MFA in fiction at UMass Amherst. His stories have appeared in Jewish Currents, The Barcelona Review, and The Brooklyn Review, among others. He currently lives in Manhattan with his wife and dog.
About the Conversation Partner:
Deborah Shapiro is the author of the novels The Sun in Your Eyes (2016, a New York Times Book Review Editors’ Choice), The Summer Demands (2019), and Consolation (2022). Her latest book is Watching the Detective (2025). Her writing has appeared in The New York Times Book Review, Los Angeles Review of Books, Sight Unseen, Chicago Magazine, Literary Hub, Washington Square Review, and elsewhere. She is the publisher of B-Side Editions and lives with her family in Chicago.

description: Here in Tributosaurus’ 25th year, we felt it imperative to include an opportunity for us to do two shows in which we become Steely Dan.You rarely if ever get the chance to see this music, performed lovingly and with precision, in a live club setting. WE WILL FOIL THEM AGAIN. We’ll recreate those vocal harmonies, keyboard orchestrations, guitar sounds, horn parts, drum and percussion fills live. We’ll assemble the band we need; the right tools for the right job.In prior years we’ve done two separate volumes of these amazing songs, more than 30 in total. We could probably do an unprecedented third volume; the catalog is that deep. Instead we’ll cull our favorites from that vast herd, ranging from Can’t Buy a Thrill through Gaucho, and also include a taste of Donald Fagen’s extraordinary solo album, The Nightfly.We consider Steely Dan the gold standard. Geddy Trezak is a pop rock artist from Hobart, Indiana. He offers a vintage sound designed and packaged for modern ears, and his music is something the world has been missing out on. He is a multi-instrumentalist and has been recording projects in his home ever since he was a teenager. He has released his first album independently and plans to release a follow up within the next year.
His career began to take shape when he was 14 when he was introduced to and learned how to record his own songs. He wears his influences on his sleeve and includes many nods to British Invasion, power pop, psychedelic, and a slew of other odds and ends from all sides of the musical spectrum. By 2020, he had formed his own band, Geddy Trezak Band, and ever since then he has been winning over crowds as an opening band and playing up to 3 hour sets around his home town. In early 2025 he released his first album Demolition and recently played shows in Chicago.
Geddy Trezak currently attends Columbia College Chicago studying Audio Arts and plans to finish out his schooling. With an album under his belt he’s keeping the experience and knowledge he has gained in mind as he writes and records his next project. Trezak has hopes of touring one day either under his own name or with a headliner and is on his way to becoming a name in the music world.
BOOMWAGON
Boomwagon is an original rock trio based in Flossmoor, IL. Their sound officially falls within the broad ‘indie rock’ sub-genre, having garnered independent label interest with the release of Mat’s (vocals, bass, principal song writer) ‘Consolation’ record release. Creative and dynamic, Boomwagon has built their fan base on equal doses of rock power, pretty harmonies, suss chords, and self-deprecating humor.
Mat (vocals, bass) is a writer, player, recordist, engineer, and progressive. Steve (guitar, vocals) is a rock music addict and refugee of Chicago bands White Paste, The Murkins, Sylvia Said, Wad, Jake & The Wranglers, and Consolation. Jim (drums), much more than a trusted time-keeper and fill-generator, uses his skill-drill training as hockey goalie and martial artist to exact the most felicitous timbre from the stroke of each cymbal. In the words of music critic Hester Bings, “The confluence of these fine fellows makes for an entertaining excursion across the lively ocean of rock goodness!”

If you’ve ever felt lost or like you didn’t quite fit, Heather sees you—and hopes you find your space at The LPs. title: Die kleine Bushaltestelle (Gerüstbau)
description:
DIRECTED BY
Kai Althoff,
Isa Genzken
WRITTEN BY
Kai Althoff,
Isa Genzken
STARRING
Kai Althoff,
Isa Genzken
Between 2007 and 2009, the artists Isa Genzken and Kai Althoff sporadically met when able and filmed the series of no-budget vignettes that became Die kleine Bushaltestelle (Gerüstbau), or "The Little Bus Stop (Scaffolding)." Between overlapping liaisons in Cologne, Berlin, and New York, Genzken and Althoff filmed in hotels, flats, and bars, performing a pas de deux at the crossroads of slapstick and philosophical dialogue.
As detectives, as babies, as sex workers, as bourgeois, as proletariat, and always irreducibly themselves, Genzken and Althoff's conversations meander between sympathy and antagonism as they blindly try to eke out a kernel of satisfaction from the lives they imitate. The numerous guises they adopt, no matter how campy, never stray far from their identities as artists navigating a world where art itself feels nearly impossible and intimacy seems hopelessly entangled with transaction. Die kleine Bushaltestelle delivers laughs to its audience with the crass intellect of John Waters or Rosa von Praunheim, while retaining the aleatory innocence of Buster Keaton, and sees Genzken and Althoff inserting themselves into the tradition of the comic duo, from Laurel and Hardy, Abbot and Costello to Nicholas and May.

title: Heartless Bastards: ‘All This Time’ 20th Anniversary
description:
Nosalve soothes quite like music does. Like the ultimate balm, it releases tension and stress and reinvigorates the spirit. With a warm patchwork of rock ‘n’ roll, psychedelia, folk, alternative, and blues, Heartless Bastards unlock healing and catharsis within their music. Whether in the studio or on stage, the Austin-based band fronted by vocalist, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, and producer Erika Wennerstrom calm as they captivate. After generating over 100 million total streams and enrapturing audiences at legendary venues such as Red Rocks Amphitheatre, the group continue to connect with listeners everywhere through boundary-breaking sonics and straight-from-the-heart lyrics.
“Music is medicine,” observes Erika. “It gives me a sense of purpose beyond just creating art. The idea someone might find comfort in it or it can actually help another person is incredible to me. I don’t know if I ever thought about it in those terms when I was younger. I’ve realized it over the years though.”
At the turn-of-the-century, Erika founded Heartless Bastards in Cincinnati, OH. Inspired by the likes of Joan Jett, Bob Dylan, Tom Petty, and more, she cut early demos in 2003, performing the bulk of the instruments herself. A bartending gig inspired the name Heartless Bastards. The bar’s touch screen game posed the question, “What is Tom Petty’s backing band?” and offered “The Heartless Bastards” as an answer option, so she accepted this humorous twist of fate and adopted it as her band’s moniker.
The band initially came to life with Stairs and Elevators in 2005, building a discography of fan favorites highlighted by All This Time [2006], The Mountain [2009], and the seminal Arrow [2012]. The latter captured #2 on the Billboard Top Independent Albums Chart, went Top 10 on the Tastemaker Albums Chart, and even cracked the Top 200. “Only For You” notably amassed north of 42.6 million Spotify streams and 17.2 million YouTube views. In the wake of the album, Time attested, “Wennerstrom’s voice is one of the cornerstones of their success. It is tender even when it is severe, and she is unabashedly soulful even when she rocks, almost as though she were at once performing a slow country ballad and singing alongside Mark Bolan from T. Rex.”
Meanwhile, 2021’s A Beautiful Life arrived to widespread praise from Uncut, Glide, and Classic Rock with Pitchfork going as far as to claim, “A Beautiful Life is her best album as a vocalist, as she finds new ways to bend her voice to different styles and sounds.” In addition to sharing the stage with The Flaming Lips, The Decemberists, Wolfmother, Lucinda Williams, and The Avett Brothers, they lit up festivals a la Bonnaroo, Lollapalooza, Austin City Limits, Newport Folk Festival, High Sierra Music Festival, and more. Through it all, Heartless Bastards constantly evolve.
“The vibe is pretty eclectic,” she goes on. “My voice ties it together. The earlier albums were a bit more garage- and punk-influenced. We’ve drawn from classic rock, indie, and folk too. I love music, and I’m always exploring sounds.”

From its beginnings as a street performance in the UK, STOMP has grown into an international sensation over the past 32 years, having performed in more than 50 countries and in front of more than 26 million people.
Created by Luke Cresswell and Steve McNicholas, STOMP continues to tour North America, Europe, Latin America and Asia following 15 years in London’s West End and 32 years at New York’s Orpheum Theatre, and lengthy sit down productions in San Francisco, Boston and Las Vegas. Throughout its life, the show has continued to change by creating
new material to bring music to everyday objects. It is safe to say you will never again look at supermarket carts or plumbing fixtures the same way or paint cans, or kitchen sinks or
STOMP, an overwhelming success marked by rave reviews, numerous awards, and sell-out engagements, is the winner of an Olivier Award for Best Choreography (London’s Tony Award), a New York Obie Award, a Drama Desk Award for Unique Theatre Experience, and a Special Citation from Best Plays.
In addition to the stage shows, STOMP has been an overwhelming success marked by rave reviews, numerous awards, an Academy Award nomination, four Emmy nominations and one Emmy Award for their acclaimed HBO special Stomp Out Loud, noteworthy TV appearances including The London 2012 Olympic Games Closing Ceremony, The Academy
Awards (produced by Quincy Jones), Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, and a series of award-winning international commercials.
The performers “make a rhythm out of anything we can get our hands on that makes a sound,” says co-founder/director Luke Cresswell. A unique combination of percussion, movement and visual comedy, STOMP has created its own inimitable, contemporary form of rhythmic expression: both household and industrial objects find new life as musical
instruments in the hands of an idiosyncratic band of body percussionists. It is a journey through sound, a celebration of the everyday and a comic interplay of characters wordlessly communicating through dance and drum.
Synchronized stiff-bristle brooms become a sweeping orchestra, eight Zippo lighters flip open and closed to create a fiery fugue; wooden poles thump and clack in a rhythmic explosion. STOMP uses everything but conventional percussion instruments – dustbins, suitcases, radiator hoses, boots, hub caps – to fill the stage with a compelling and unique act that
is often imitated but never duplicated.
Critics and audiences have raved: “STOMP is as crisp and exuberant as if it had opened yesterday,” says The New York Times. The San Francisco Chronicle declares “STOMP has a beat that just won’t quit!” The Los Angeles Times exclaims: “Electrifying! Triumphs in the infinite variety of the human experience.” “A phenomenal show! Bashing, crashing, smashing, swishing, banging and kicking – a joyous invention!” says the Chicago Tribune.

The DuPage Community Jazz Ensembles and Director Matt Shevitz are excited to collaborate with internationally renowned jazz clarinetist Anat Cohen for their December 3 concert! The Chicago Tribune recently praised Cohen for the “lyric beauty of her tone, easy fluidity of her technique and extroverted manner of her delivery make this music accessible to all.” The evening will feature such works by such composers as Duke Ellington, Luis Bonfa, and Lil Hardin, as well as arrangements of some of Cohen’s original works. Joining Cohen and the ensembles will be this semester’s Artists-in-Residence Jimmy Farace (saxophone), Josh Torrey (trombone), Emily Kuhn (trumpet), and Terry Bartolotta (guitar).
Program:
