Clarinetist-saxophonist Anat Cohen has won hearts and minds around the globe with her expressive virtuosity and magnetic stage presence, earning esteem both as a musician’s musician and as a performer who charms new recruits to the jazz art like few others. With her acclaimed albums, sold-out world tours and Grammy Award nominations adding up over the past two and a half decades — not to mention the glowing profiles by such totemic outlets as NPR’s Fresh Air and The New York Times — it has become apparent that the Brooklyn-based Anat has evolved into one of the music’s great border-bounding leaders, as not only an artist but as an educator, an ambassador. At the core of this, there is always her jubilant, ever-exploratory music-making, as a soloist, bandleader, collaborator and composer.
Cohen has been named Clarinetist of the Year by the Jazz Journalists Association every year since 2007, and she has also been the top clarinetist in both the readers and critics polls in DownBeat every year since 2011. She released her 21st album—Bloom—in 2024 with her small group, Quartetinho. In March 2025, she released the live album Interaction on her Anzic Records label, uniting her family band The 3 Cohens (with brothers Avishai and Yuval) alongside Germany’s WDR Big Band. Conducted and arranged by frequent collaborator Oded Lev-Ari—who also works with Anat’s Grammy-nominated Tentet—the concert recording showcases the 10-piece ensemble’s signature collaborative flair.
As an international presence, Anat has performed from across North and South America to Europe, Asia and India, headlining at the Newport and Umbria jazz festivals as well as at Chicago’s Symphony Center and such hallowed clubs as New York’s Village Vanguard. Anat has worked with artists from Latin jazz star Paquito D’Rivera and breakout vocalist Cécile McLorin Salvant to arthouse pianist Fred Hersch and the all-star, all-woman band Artemis, among others. With her brothers in The 3 Cohens, she has toured the world and recorded five albums. Anat teaches at the Stanford University Jazz Workshop in California and The New School in Manhattan, among other institutions, and she has been Jazz Artist-in-Residence at Columbia University’s Zuckerman Institute.
The DuPage Community Jazz Ensembles performs programs throughout the academic year as well as numerous off‐campus performances. The ensemble has accompanied guest artists such as Melissa Aldana, Wycliffe Gordon, Ignacio Berroa, Carl Allen, Dee Alexander, Fareed Haque, Jens Lindemann, Victor Garcia, and Mark Colby, is a frequent presence at the Elmhurst University Jazz Festival, has performed at the Jazz Showcase in Chicago, and in 2004 was recognized by the United States House of Representatives for its work on behalf of the Armed Forces Children’s Education Fund. Its repertoire spans more than a century of large jazz ensemble compositions, including original work from members of the ensemble.
About the Director: Matt Shevitz is an in-demand musician in the jazz, blues, and popular music scenes of Chicago area. He has performed alongside such internationally renowned jazz musicians as Dick Hyman, Ignacio Berroa, Howard Levy, Frank Capp, and Frank Wess along with blues/roots rock guitarist Eric Lindell and Ropeadope Records artists Spare Parts. Shevitz has performed at Jazz in the Park Festival (Milwaukee), Waterfront Blues Festival (Portland), Chicago Blues Festival, Lollapalooza and House of Blues in Chicago. Matt is a contributor to DownBeat Magazine since 2009 with articles analyzing transcriptions of great jazz solos as well as jazz theory and effective practice habits. Matt is a professor and the Director of Jazz Ensembles at the College of DuPage in Glen Ellyn, IL. He received a Doctor of Musical Arts in Jazz Performance degree from the Univ. of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Master of Music in Jazz Pedagogy from Northwestern Univ. and a Bachelor of Science in Music from the Univ. of Oregon.

description:
2026 Christmas Tour Thoughts
One December, not long after Over the Rhine began recording and touring, we were invited to perform some seasonal songs on a public radio station. We worked up a few carols and traditional tunes. It actually felt really good and conjured up an unusual mix of feelings from childhood: innocence, loss, wonder, joy, sadness. I think we were surprised.
People must have tuned into the radio broadcast, because we began receiving inquiries as to whether we had recorded any of our Christmas songs. In December of 1996 – can it really be 30 years ago? – we recorded and released our first song cycle of some of the Christmas carols that still haunted us. We included a few original tunes and called our wintry mix The Darkest Night Of The Year. Folks began snatching up copies and seemed to agree that they hadn't heard anything quite like it.
We began playing concerts around the Midwest every December and found that the rooms were usually packed full of people who had bundled in out of the cold. If you stepped outside during intermission, you could make ghosts with your breath in the crisp night air. And it was dark - oh so dark: a time of year with its own music.
A decade later, in 2006, we released our first full collection of original Christmas/holiday songs called Snow Angels. What is it about Christmas music and the undeniable gravitational pull it exerts on some songwriters? So many Christmas songs have already been written. I think we remain genuinely curious about the ones that haven't yet been written.
We continued to tour every December and these special year-winding-down concerts began to feel like an annual tradition - gatherings of extended musical family, without whom, we'd be homeless.
We released our third holiday album of original songs, Blood Oranges In The Snow, in December of 2014. One enthusiastic fan wrote to us, I just love your new Christmas album, Blood On The Oranges. We're dark but not that dark.
On our 2026 tour, we will be leaning into some harmonies and making an intimate but hopefully holy ruckus. It won't be all Christmas music: we'll certainly mix in tunes from many of our records along the way. But hopefully it's still true: hopefully, you haven't heard anything quite like it.
We hope you'll join us,
Linford Detweiler
With Karin close by
Nowhere Else

title: 2nd Set With Mario Abney
description:
As a Chicago native, Mario Abney’s trumpet playing fuses traditional and extended techniques in an inventive way. His uniquely personal vision for music endows it with an infinite array of tonal colors. He is recognized for his ability to create pure musical dialogues and hear music in a universally spiritual way. These qualities make him one of New Orleans’ most pioneering young jazz musicians.
Trumpeter, composer and bandleader Mario Abney’s musical career began at age 7 when he was introduced to the piano by his uncle Arthur. Influenced by both his uncle’s playing and the musical background of his church, Abney developed a love and fascination for music that grew throughout his years in high school. It was during this time that his interest turned from piano and drums to wind instruments; however, he continued to hone his percussion skills by playing drums for church services.
Mario’s first encounter with jazz was when he heard the sounds of trumpeter Wynton Marsalis. This sparked a fascination and soon Mario began to explore music by Louis Armstrong, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis and other great trumpet players who established this genre.
Fast forwarding to 2024, Mario Abney is once again gracing the stages of his beloved hometown Chicago. From iconic venues to up-and-coming spots, he’s become a regular feature with fans eagerly anticipating each and every performance.

title: Blueprint
description:
Blueprint is the kind of improv that keeps audiences AND players on their toes. Each week, a different cast member designs a bold new improv format that their fellow performers will learn about at the same time as the crowd. Expect the unexpected as we build something completely original, live, right before your eyes.
Past forms have included: 
Improvised Severance - Guided by two internal "staff members," three performers are physically out of the room, while three others perform as their innies, and every 5 minutes, the two swapped. Can they make sense of their outies? and versa?
Understudies - In a longform narrative, each player on stage knows that they will eventually understudy another player in the show. The lights change and they have to embody a different player, and each time the lights change, they can select another player to embody.
Overachiever - Three 2-person monoscenes happen on stage, utilizing the same physical space, but taking place in categorically different spaces. They must navigate space atop of and around one another while keeping connection to their partner.
Improvised Heist - Ocean's Eleven, eat your heart out! Our players hit the major plot points of a heist and improvise their way through - initial idea, building the team, planning the heist, executing, and the aftermath

He has since been a fixture in the Chicago jazz community, leading quartets and quintets, and collaborating with notable musicians such as Todd Herbert, Art Davis, Tim Davis, and Kevin O’Connell. His style blends solid, melodic bass lines with inventive, exploratory solos, influenced in part by the legacy of Oscar Pettiford.
Pardo’s work is marked by a “clearly delineated bass” that both anchors the rhythm and ventures into melodic exploration. His 2010 album I Get the Message, Volume 1: The Genius of Oscar Pettiford is a tribute to Pettiford, featuring collaborations with violinist Mark Feldman, tenorist Ron Dewar, pianist Jeremy Kahn, and drummer Bill “Bugs” Cochran.
Pardo is never slavish in his homages to his hero; rather, he puts his own contemporary stamp on the material throughout. Nor does he leave any doubt that he’s a take-charge kind of guy; not content for a minute to play a supporting role, he’s a smart enough leader to know what he’s got in these musicians and to allow them their own say in these lovingly rendered interpretations.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.

title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.

Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: A Sneak Peek on the Dark Side: First DarkSide-20k Analysis Workshop
location: The University of Chicago John W. Boyer Center in Paris
description:
A wide range of astrophysical and cosmological measurements indicates that the universe is filled with far more matter than what we can account for by looking around us. This excess matter is called dark matter and, while it is thought to be constituted by a new, exotic species of elementary particle, its nature remains unknown — making it one of the biggest puzzles in modern particle physics and cosmology.
 DarkSide-20k (DS-20k) is an experiment currently under construction at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso, beneath the Apennine Mountains in Italy. It aims to detect the potential feeble interactions of dark matter particles using an innovative detector featuring a 50-tonne target of specially sourced argon, extracted from underground gas reservoirs in Colorado and depleted in the radioactive isotopes that typically contaminate argon extracted from air. This massive, low-background target, instrumented as a two-phase Time Projection Chamber, is expected to feature a sensitivity to dark matter exceeding that of any currently running experiment.
 The event, held at the University of Chicago’s John W. Boyer Center in Paris, is the first collaboration-wide analysis workshop — previous workshops were much smaller in scale — and aims to kickstart the finalization of the study of DS-20k’s sensitivity to dark matter. By the end of the workshop, the organizers aims to be able to run the full simulation and analysis pipeline, evaluating the final sensitivity of the experiment while accounting for the finer details of the detector response. The workshop will also train a new cohort of researchers to become core members of the analysis team in preparation to early data. The event is organized by the International Institute of Research in Paris, with primary support from The University of Chicago and the Université Paris Cité, and with the participation of AstroCeNT.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Pierre Bismuth: Love Bless America
location: Neubauer Collegium for Culture and Society
description:
This exhibition features new works by the French artist and filmmaker Pierre Bismuth. The centerpiece is a long-form meditative film documenting a creative collaboration between Joshua Abrams and Sharon Udoh, two leading figures from Chicago’s jazz and improvised music scene. Bismuth tasked them with composing a 21st-century spiritual based on a lyrical hymn he wrote for the project. The film traces the magic and workaday practice of “inspiration,” taking the traditions of religious music as a point of departure for a multi-layered reflection on love, music, and the divine. In addition to this new film, Bismuth will present a series of digital images resembling American flags emblazoned with lyrics from the hymn.

Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding.

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

title: The Whiteness Between Us
description:
In this virtual conversation, Noémie Ndiaye and Yunah Kae discuss the role that theatre played in the development of European race-making in the early modern period.
Over the course of the seventeenth century, European drama was an important tool for whiteness to imagine itself at the top of an aspirational structure of power relations. Indeed, that structure could only be aspirational at a time when Europeans were profoundly divided along easily racializable religious and ethnic lines, and when their sovereignty was threatened by the Ottoman empire. It was to strengthen this emerging consciousness of racial whiteness, Noémie Ndiaye argues, that European drama engaged in a form of racial triangulation, fitting Muslim, Jewish, Indigenous, Romani, and Asian characters into a spurious black/white racial binary.
Focusing on English, Spanish, and French drama from 1580 to 1715, The Whiteness Between Us shows how plays became a crucial tool to position not only black people but any non-white community in the new racial architecture that white supremacy sought to build. Ndiaye reveals the stage of this era as a space for wish fulfillment, enabling participants to imagine and work towards a whiter future.

title: CEGU Colloquium: Hayley Birss
description:
Outside of History: Frontier Imaginaries, Temporal Amnesia, and Anglo-Canadian Nationalism in a Melting Arctic
 Hayley Birss, PhD Student in CHSS and Anthropology)
 What happens when an environmental imaginary—a frozen frontier that has anchored a hegemonic political formation for over a century—begins to melt? This paper takes that question seriously by examining how the dominant Anglo-Canadian national imaginary persists through ecological and sovereignty crises. To do this, the paper draws on Benedict Anderson’s theory of imagined communities, Michael Rogin’s distinction between the form and content of political demonology, and Orit Halpern’s conceptualization of the Smartness Mandate to interpret Prime Minister Mark Carney’s recent speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. I argue that the Arctic functions not simply as a biotrope of national identity but as a technology of temporal amnesia. The Arctic materializes a frontier imaginary that stabilizes settler sovereignty by positioning Anglo-Canadian identity outside (not before) the homogenous causality of industrial modernity and its History. In the early twentieth century, the Group of Seven’s anti-modernist landscapes exemplify the deliberate erasure of all human presence from Arctic landscapes, naturalizing settler authority by rendering colonial occupation outside (not before) History; in the twenty-first century, the Smartness Mandate’s “demo-logic” governs through a futurity that brackets the past circumstance indeterminate and irrelevant. Although there appears to be a transition in content—from the vast timeless wilderness of the anti-modern imaginary to the networked, speculative futurity of technocratic governance after Carney’s “rupture in world order”—temporal amnesia is a consistent political form that naturalizes Anglo-Canadian hegemonic settler-nationalism and erasure of Indigenous and Inuit sovereignty.

title: Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? Gallery Hours
description:
Arts + Public Life at the University of Chicago presents Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? a new exhibition by Chicago artist Candace Hunter centered on the construction of the Dan Ryan Expressway and the Black communities displaced in its path. Now embedded within Chicago’s physical and social fabric, the Dan Ryan Expressway obscures both the choices that produced it and the lives reorganized around it. The construction disrupted the ordinary intimacies through which a place becomes home: routes traveled, neighbors known, businesses frequented, porches gathered on.
 Through photographic collage, architectural fragments, archival materials, sound, sculptural interventions, and oral histories, Hunter moves between what is documented and what is remembered. The work resists the idea that displacement can be understood solely through statistics.
 The series builds on the Memory Teas Candace hosted during her APL residency, which gathered first-person accounts from Black Chicagoans who remember the Dan Ryan’s construction and the neighborhoods transformed by it. Rather than asking these memories to complete the historical record, Hunter allows them to stay partial, layered, and unresolved.
 While centered on Chicago’s South Side, the history at the heart of Intentionality, 1960 reaches beyond the city. Across the United States, highway construction, redevelopment, and urban renewal reshaped Black communities, often presenting profound social and spatial disruption as necessary progress. Intentionality, 1960 invites audiences to see those histories not as isolated events but as part of a larger American story.
 Intentionality, 1960 will be accompanied by Threshold: Conversations on the Stoop, a series of public dialogues on the front porch within the exhibition between Candace and scholars to dive into topics related to the exhibition. The Threshold conversations are presented with support from the Office of the Provost Diversity and Inclusion team, in partnership with the Chicago Forum for Free Inquiry and Expression.
 Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? will be on view from September 24-December 12 in the Arts + Public Life Gallery Space located in the Arts Incubator at 301 E. Garfield Blvd.

In a world where our personal and professional lives are increasingly intertwined, everyone is negotiating - at work with managers, clients, teams, and vendors, and at home with family or friends, and even with ourselves.

New Rules of Negotiation offers a modern, compassionate roadmap to negotiating with confidence, so you can get what truly matters most to you.

Beyond client representation, Kristen trains businesses on workplace compliance and culture, and frequently speaks to professional organizations on negotiation and leadership topics. title: CANCELED: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Today’s 4:30 pm tour is closed to the public. Please visit us again next quarter.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

Intrigue, corruption, betrayal, survival: the walls of the maze are closing in.
The latest from Oscar® nominated writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan), Cannes Grand Prix winner MINOTAUR is a twist-laden parable for our times.
Russia, 2022. Amidst the comfortable trappings of affluence and domesticity, corporate executive Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) finds himself under siege on all fronts. At home, he is haunted by suspicions that his increasingly distant wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is unfaithful. At work, he contends with a demand from local authorities to draft a quota of employees for the war in Ukraine. Desperate to keep his hands clean, Gleb struggles to reassert control even as the collapse of his carefully ordered life seems fated to accelerate toward violence.
A pressure cooker in cinematic form, MINOTAUR uncovers and indicts the heart of societal darkness with searing clarity. Uniting intimately-drawn performances and stark visual power, France’s Best International Feature Film entry to the 99th Academy Awards® is peerless work from an indisputable master.

The Cornelia Arts Building open its doors to the public for their December Open House event where visitors can see working artist studios and purchase fine art and unique artisan made gifts directly from the artists! The Cornelia Arts Building December Open House opens on Friday December 4, from 5 - 9 pm, and Saturday December 5, from 12 to 4 pm, and is located at 1800 West Cornelia Avenue, Chicago, Illinois. title: Kintsugi for Beginners
description:
Fri, Dec 04
Heritage Museum of Asian Art
Learn the art of Kintsugi with artifact restoration expert Mami Takahashi. This workshop includes free museum admission. We recommend arriving between 5:00 and 5:30 p.m. to enjoy the galleries before the workshop begins.
Dec 04, 2026, 6:00 PM – 8:30 PM
Heritage Museum of Asian Art, 3500 S Morgan St, Chicago, IL 60609, USA
This beginner’s workshop introduces participants to the art of Kintsugi, a traditional Japanese technique of repairing broken ceramics with gold-infused lacquer, emphasizing the beauty of imperfections. Using a small porcelain or ceramic plate provided by the instructor, attendees will learn fundamental techniques with food-safe materials, including artificial Urushi resin, epoxy putty, and ceramic glue. Designed for those interested in Kintsugi, this hands-on experience offers a safe and accessible way to explore its philosophy of resilience and transformation.
This event is a collaboration between Japanese Culture Center and Heritage Museum of Chicago.
Artist Bio:
Mami Takahashi is a Japanese multidisciplinary artist and scholar in Chicago. She received her MFA in Contemporary Studio Practice from Portland State University in 2013 and earned a BFA in Japanese Painting from Joshibi University of Art and Design in Japan.
With ongoing artistic research, practice, and teaching, Takahashi explores different approaches to actualize Japanese aesthetics to enhance cultural perspectives in many U.S. communities. She is expanding her creativity to incorporate more specific discourses around society, past and present via a lens of Japanese art. Takahashi also aims to connect Japan and Chicago by teaching traditional and modern art-making techniques.
Kintsugi is a traditional Japanese lacquer/Urushi art form in which gold mixed with natural lacquer-tree sap is used to repair broken ceramics. The practice of Kintsugi highlights the break rather than erasing it and emphasizes that the break, or trauma, is what makes the ceramics more valuable.
Here is a quote about Kintsugi from Linda Muller, a certified life coach:
“Kintsugi is based on the philosophy that breakage and repair are something to celebrate – embracing flaws and imperfections creates a stronger and more beautiful piece of art. Using this as a metaphor for healing ourselves teaches us an important lesson: Sometimes in the process of repairing what feels broken, we become more unique, beautiful and resilient. Kintsugi can be a way to reframe personal challenges. Reminding us that we’re not a victim of our circumstances. Showing us that we can come out on the other side stronger.”
In this beginner’s workshop, participants will learn the basic technique of Kintsugi on a small porcelain plate or a small ceramic plate, which the instructor will provide, to understand the fundamentals of this process. All materials including adhesives in the workshop will be food-safe. We will also use an artificial Urushi (the natural resin/glue collected from the lacquer tree) sap for this beginner’s class, which is safe to touch without allergy reactions.
Note: This workshop also uses epoxy putty and ceramic glue. Some remnants from these may stay on participants' fingers. Finger covers will be provided but it could make a difficult to work on the details.

Piedmont Dinner with Guest Chef Fernanda Giamello and Piedmont Historian Daniela Viberti
The Night:
An immersion in Piedmont. Join us as guest Chef Fernanda Giamello teaches you how to make a few famous dishes from the Piedmont region of Italy. Who will teach:
Fernanda Giamello | Chef & Cooking Instructor
Raised on a family farm in Barbaresco, Fernanda Giamello brings the culinary traditions of Piedmont to life through recipes and techniques learned alongside her parents. From handmade pasta to the region’s beloved hazelnut pastries, her cooking reflects a deep connection to local ingredients and family traditions. Featured in Bake from Scratch, Fernanda welcomes guests from around the world into her kitchen near Alba, sharing the food, stories, and hospitality of her native region.
Daniela Viberti | Culinary Collaborator & Piedmont Guide
An experienced guide based in Alba, Daniela Viberti brings extensive knowledge of Piedmont’s food, wines, and cultural traditions. Her connection to E. Pira & Figli, the Barolo estate associated with celebrated winemaker Chiara Boschis, adds a firsthand perspective on the region’s wine community.

title: Cuba & Alaska
description:
In Yegor Troyanovsky’s Cuba & Alaska, the frontlines of Kharkiv, Ukraine are framed through the queasy lenses of helmet-attached GoPros, shaky phone cameras, and intimate video calls; the ongoing drone of war processed through the hands of those closest to it. The eponymous pair, Cuba and Alaska – formally, Yulia and Oleksandra – are this story’s protagonists, two volunteer combat medics who approach the ongoing invasion with grit, tenacity, and an extraordinary sense of humor, shouldering the responsibility of bringing much-needed levity to their everyday lives. As the war grinds on, the two rely on one another to maintain their senses of self while enlisting themselves in the daily pursuit of liberation.
 When tragedy strikes and their stories diverge, Cuba and Alaska are suddenly thrust into an even greater unknown – who are they without the other, without their bond forged on the battlefield? How can they bridge the gap between their life at war and life as they knew it? What will remain after these transformative and destructive seasons at war?
 Troyanovsky approaches this story of sisterhood and bravery with astonishing sensitivity and the gentleness of an old friend; this story, after all, continues to unfold beyond the confines of the screen. Today, nearly a year after the film’s initial release, Cuba and Alaska are still enmeshed in the Ukrainian conflict; their home is still under attack. In this uniquely urgent documentation of a profound moment of unrest, Cuba and Alaska are larger than life, exposing the horrors, absurdity, and mundanity of war from their own perspective. (Yegor Troyanovsky, Belgium, Ukraine, France, 2025, 93 minutes, DCP)
 Presented in partnership with People in Need and One World Film Festival in observance of International Human Rights Day, with protagonists Cuba and Alaska in person. With support from the Pozen Family Center for Human Rights.
 Film Studies Center events are free and open to the public. Doors open thirty minutes prior to showtime.

description:
DARKEST HOUR
A bastard child born of the mid 90s punk/metal/hardcore movement, Washington, DC’s DARKEST HOUR combine the passion, energy, and soul of punk/hardcore with the style, speed, vengeance and fury of melodic speed/thrash/death metal.
DARKEST HOUR have helped defined the entire New Wave of American Metal sound as one of the pioneers of modern metal/core. A sound that gave the metal and hardcore/punk world the revitalization it surely needed. This style blended the raw, hardcore punk of the 80s, with the Scandinavian death metal of the 90s and forged a sound that would later become the template for modern metal.
Since their inception 23 years ago, Darkest Hour has released 9 studio full lengths (via 11 different record labels), appeared in major motion pictures, US television shows, video games, and have toured the world extensively covering 6 of the 7 continents.
Darkest Hour is: Mike Schleibaum – Guitar John Henry – Vocals Nico Santora – Guitar Aaron Deal – Bass Travis Orbin – Drums
JUDICIARY
Balancing traditionally timeless grit with 21st century gusto, Judiciary hammer out hardcore grooves at breakneck thrash speeds. The Texas quintet—Jake Collinson [vocals], Juan Vazquez [bass], Austin Looney [drums], Jimmy LaDue [guitar], and Israel Garza [guitar]—wield a searing signature style unlike anything in heavy music. With calculated intensity, it bludgeons without compromise, draws back for a breath, and strikes again even harder.
Grinding full force since 2015, the band unleashed the EP The Axis of Equality in 2016, a split EP with Mortality Rate in 2017, and finally, their first full-length record Surface Noise with Closed Casket Activities in 2019. Of the latter, Revolver exclaimed, “More so than many other bands in their orbit, the quintet excels at writing riffs that hang on through any one track without faltering,” while Stereogum raved, “It fucking rips.” Beyond highlights such as “Stronger Than Thou” [feat. Bryan Garris of Knocked Loose] and “Temple” [feat. Brody King of God’s Hate], their standout single “Social Crusade” signaled success for what the band had set out to accomplish with their first LP.
Citing influences such as Slayer’s God Hates Us All and Chimaira’s The Impossibility of Reason as well as “a ton of Machine Head,” Judiciary perfected their blend of metal and hardcore on the 2023 second full-length record, Flesh + Blood [Closed Casket Activities]. Flesh + Blood was recorded and produced by Arthur Rizk [Power Trip, Cavalera Conspiracy] in August of 2021 before GRAMMY® Award-winner Will Putney [Body Count, Vein] handled mixing and mastering, and has since received the praise of Stereogum, Revolver, BrooklynVegan, Invisible Oranges, and more.

title: Tributosaurus becomes... Steely Dan!
description: Here in Tributosaurus’ 25th year, we felt it imperative to include an opportunity for us to do two shows in which we become Steely Dan.You rarely if ever get the chance to see this music, performed lovingly and with precision, in a live club setting. It’s absurd to attempt! Every time we’ve done Steely Dan, there is a special section for a certain subsection of fans with arms folded, waiting expectantly for us to make mistakes. WE WILL FOIL THEM AGAIN. We’ll recreate those vocal harmonies, keyboard orchestrations, guitar sounds, horn parts, drum and percussion fills live. We’ll assemble the band we need; the right tools for the right job.In prior years we’ve done two separate volumes of these amazing songs, more than 30 in total. We could probably do an unprecedented third volume; the catalog is that deep. Instead we’ll cull our favorites from that vast herd, ranging from Can’t Buy a Thrill through Gaucho, and also include a taste of Donald Fagen’s extraordinary solo album, The Nightfly.We consider Steely Dan the gold standard. Come bask in that music with us, on one or both of these two nights.

Most recently, Steve wrote and directed the semi autobiographical feature film about his early years in stand up comedy called "The Opening Act". Starring a roster of who's who in the stand up world (Bill Burr, Cedric the Entertainer, Russell Peters, Tom Segura, Whitney Cummings, Ken Jeong, Jimmy O Yang, Iliza and many others) the film was revered by stand up fans and critics alike sitting at 86% Fresh on Rotten Tomatoes.

title: Cuba & Alaska
description:
In Yegor Troyanovsky’s Cuba & Alaska, the frontlines of Kharkiv, Ukraine are framed through the queasy lenses of helmet-attached GoPros, shaky phone cameras, and intimate video calls; the ongoing drone of war processed through the hands of those closest to it. The eponymous pair, Cuba and Alaska – formally, Yulia and Oleksandra – are this story’s protagonists, two volunteer combat medics who approach the ongoing invasion with grit, tenacity, and an extraordinary sense of humor, shouldering the responsibility of bringing much-needed levity to their everyday lives. As the war grinds on, the two rely on one another to maintain their senses of self while enlisting themselves in the daily pursuit of liberation.
When tragedy strikes and their stories diverge, Cuba and Alaska are suddenly thrust into an even greater unknown – who are they without the other, without their bond forged on the battlefield? How can they bridge the gap between their life at war and life as they knew it? What will remain after these transformative and destructive seasons at war?
Troyanovsky approaches this story of sisterhood and bravery with astonishing sensitivity and the gentleness of an old friend; this story, after all, continues to unfold beyond the confines of the screen. Today, nearly a year after the film’s initial release, Cuba and Alaska are still enmeshed in the Ukrainian conflict; their home is still under attack. In this uniquely urgent documentation of a profound moment of unrest, Cuba and Alaska are larger than life, exposing the horrors, absurdity, and mundanity of war from their own perspective. (Yegor Troyanovsky, Belgium, Ukraine, France, 2025, 93 minutes, DCP)
Presented in partnership with People in Need and One World Film Festival in observance of International Human Rights Day, with protagonists Cuba and Alaska in person. With support from the Pozen Family Center for Human Rights.

Pianist Jeffrey Panko has received critical acclaim as both solo and collaborative artist throughout the United States and Europe. Earning degrees in piano performance from the Oberlin College Conservatory of Music and the DePaul University School of Music, Panko was awarded top prizes in the Society of American Musicians’ Piano Competition (Chicago) and the Frinna Awerbuch International Piano Competition (New York).
Following a concert tour of Poland where he was honored by the United States with the title of Cultural Ambassador, Panko was invited by the City of Chicago to present a Chopin recital for the visiting Lech Walesa and other Polish dignitaries. Panko has also been featured in performances at Carnegie Hall, Weill Hall, Lincoln Center Library, WQXR Radio (New York), is a frequent performer on WFMT Radio (Chicago), and appeared in Symphony Center playing the music of Steven Sondheim for Mr. Sondheim.
An Artist Faculty member of the New Music School piano faculty in Chicago, Panko also serves as Minister of Music and as Artistic Director of the Music at Bethel Concert Series for Bethel United Church of Christ in Elmhurst.
Timothy Archbold is an Australian cellist currently playing with the Wisconsin Chamber Orchestra, Camerata Chicago, Skylight Theater, and as associate principal with the Northwest Indiana Symphony Orchestra. He received his undergraduate degree in music from the University of Melbourne, Australia, then studied chamber music and cello performance in Germany for five years at the Hochschule fur Kunste in Bremen and European Chamber Music Academy in Hannover. He went on to receive his master’s degree in music from Wichita State University where he played with the Graduate String Quartet and the Wichita Symphony.
He is currently freelancing in the Chicagoland area. In addition to his classical performing, he enjoys a wide range of styles from playing in a Latin jazz band, appearing with worship bands to accompanying dancers in Cerqua Rivera. He is also a part of musical program for late-stage alzheimer patients studying the effects of music on the brain. Timothy has a large studio of private students and coaches honor chamber music ensembles with Elgin Youth Symphony Orchestra and several area high schools.
When not doing cello stuff, Timothy enjoys crossfit and spending time with his wife and three girls Eleanor, Lucy, and Abigail.

title: Bedouine
location: Gary and Laura Maurer Concert Hall Presents
description:
As a child, if you're lucky, summer afternoons stretch out like a yawn, pool waves are as warm and engulfing as a blanket, the safety of your mother's arms feels endless. On her new album, Neon Summer Skin, Bedouine, the project of Azniv Korkejian, explores this feeling of safety long before one can fully understand the concept. Written with vivid, honest and intimate imagery after visiting her family in Saudi Arabia, it tells the story of family and upbringing, and mourns the end of her childhood. There is a singular resonance and newfound heft in this music previously unheard in Bedouine's discography.
Bedouine is known for making gentle, lilting folk songs that build fingerpicked guitar melodies into tsunamis of emotion. Her masterful songwriting and timeless melodies have earned her praise from publications like Pitchfork, who said her music “boasts a surreal calm and lived in glow,” and Rolling Stone, who lauded her “humble folk-pop brilliance,” plus an NPR Tiny Desk Concert, and tours with the likes of Fleet Foxes and Father John Misty.
https://www.bedouinemusic.com/
Other Delights. Ferncore. Easy glistening. Screwtop exotica. Cocobilly. A band with such remarkable cross-genre fluency that no single descriptor captures their essence, and new terminologies emerge.
Other Delights was forged in Los Angeles in 2024 by drummer and producer Robin MacMillan, singer-songwriter Adron, bassist Aaron Olson ( LA Takedown, Musical Tracing Ensemble) and Andrew Dorsett (Lake, Tucker Zimmerman) on keys. All shared passions for dollar-bin lounge, '60s Euro cinema soundtracks, bubblegum psychedelia and Tropicália. Shaking off the hangover of recent cynic-donimated decades where "extra" is a pejorative, Other Delights go bananas - Adron's vocals frequently soar into operatic ranges. MacMillan's blocks and bells conjure wild, hallucinatory, even cartoonish spaces. Olson's harmonica serves hammy and heartfelt in equal measure. Dorsett's keys sweep and sparkle in exquisite melodrama. “Yes, and," indeed.
https://www.instagram.com/otherdelightsplease/

title: Mike Cooley (of Drive-by Truckers)
description: Mike Cooley is an American guitarist, singer, and songwriter, best known as a member of the Southern rock band Drive-By Truckers. The Alabama musical style blends elements of rock, country, and Americana, and he is recognized for his sharp, evocative lyrics and distinctive guitar work. As one of the band's primary songwriters, Cooley has written numerous iconic tracks for Drive-By Truckers, with his songs often exploring themes of personal introspection, Southern identity, and social commentary. Alongside bandmate Patterson Hood, Cooley has been a driving force behind the band's evolution since their formation in the late 1990s, contributing to their gritty, honest sound and critical success. In addition to his work with the band, Cooley has pursued a solo career, releasing his debut solo album The Fool on Every Corner in December 2012. The album showcases his storytelling prowess and ability to create poignant, introspective songs with a more stripped-down, intimate sound compared to his work with Drive-By Truckers. Known for his wit and keen observational style, Cooley's solo work highlights his versatility as an artist, cementing his place as an influential figure in contemporary American roots music.

Michael Ross, a native of Chicago, IL. was encouraged at an early age to take private guitar lessons at the Chicago School of Music. While advancing his studies in music at Loop Jr. College and Chicago Conservatory of Music, Michael performed at several of Chicago’s local jazz clubs. He soon later became the staff guitarist for the first New York Broadway National Touring Company’s production of “The Wiz,” that toured across the United States. Michael’s sound is true to the heart – filled with emotions, style, technique. description:

Who are we underneath it all? Behind the image we project to our communities, beyond the cloaks of grime we accumulate while living in the heart of an empire, who is revealed when we wash it all away? Those are the questions that inspired rapper and Chicago native Mykele Deville for his second studio album, Rings Around The Tub.
Mykele, a full bodied performer and gripping MC from the city’s westside, focused the music on himself as he crafted each song between the tense years of 2019 – 2023. On the surface the record chronicles his personal developments as an artist, community member, and prospective father. Underneath, Rings Around The Tub acts as an intimate check-in and cleanse for the creative soul. It is the soundtrack for the uncertain black millennial who have endured the isolation of a global pandemic, inflation, insurrection, and the cyclical rhythms of a discordant future.
Daryn Alexus, a singer/songwritter based in Chicago, has spent much of her life on the stage. Be it in theater productions, choral performances, or musicals, she was consistently involved in the arts. Taking time over the years to focus solely on music and writing original material, Daryn bridges the gap between her love for Disco, Rock N Roll, Soul, RnB, and Pop music. She has since released a project titled GREEN that she describes as Sole Music. Daryn is only just beginning and looking forward to spreading love with her music.
Malci is a Chicago-based rapper, producer, and co-founder of Why? Records. Known for intricate wordplay and unconventional references, Malci’s lyrics explore themes of anxiety, identity, and the absurdities of the human experience.
As a producer, Malci approaches hip-hop as an opportunity for sonic exploration, building distinctive musical landscapes. With recent projects like Black Seinfeld., a duo with Chicago rapper Fluidi-G, Malci showcases a playful, experimental approach to art rap utilizing bass-heavy production, absurdist humor, and observations of everyday life.

title: Abe Partridge and Clark Paterson
description:
Abe Partridge is a heralded musician, singer/songwriter, visual artist, storyteller and documentarian based in Mobile, Alabama. Since the release of his debut album Cotton Fields and Blood for Days in 2018, Partridge has toured relentlessly, including several tours throughout Europe. He is a regular at several great music festivals such as the 30a Songwriters Fest, and the Laurel Cove Music Fest as well as listening rooms across the country including the legendary Bluebird Cafe in Nashville, Eddies Attic in Atlanta, and Duke's in Indianapolis. Recently, he toured extensively with Matthew Sweet, Drivin' N Cryin', and Dar Williams in support of his latest release Love in the Dark. He has performed on several syndicated NPR radio programs including, Mountain Stage and Woodsongs Old Time Radio Hour. Partridge along with co-producer Ferrill Gibbs created the Alabama Astronaut podcast, where Abe attempts to properly record songs previously undocumented at holiness, serpent-handling churches in Appalachia. It was in the Top Ten documentary podcasts on Apple Podcasts within days of its release and now has over 100k downloads and a 4.9-star rating.
Clark Paterson doesn’t write songs from a safe distance. He writes them from the middle of the wreckage: hospital rooms, court dates, bar shifts at Robert's Western World, old farmhouses mid-restoration, garages cluttered with vintage car parts, and the strange emotional territory between heartbreak, survival, and redemption.Raised on his family’s farm near Sandusky, Michigan, Paterson grew up around hard work, old machinery, and the kind of rural honesty that eventually found its way into his songs. Before settling in East Nashville, he studied at the Old Town School of Folk Music in Chicago and then traveled the world with a backpack and a guitar, absorbing stories everywhere he landed. In Clark’s words “I became a backpacker dude and had a good run. I’ve played country music in the most unlikely places. I’ve also had the shit beat out of me and been deported.” Those experiences shaped a songwriter who can move seamlessly between grit and poetry. Humor and heartbreak."

title: Leopold Procession
description:
Artists from the Poor Farm Experiment with members of Deeply Choir, directed by Chris Wood and accompanied on dulcimer by Corey Smith, will lead a public procession from the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) to SAIC Galleries, carrying objects, props, and garments from their project Leopold Benches: A P(o)or(t)ch Theater. Departing from the plaza of the MCA at 11:00 a.m., the company will proceed to The Poetry Foundation, the Driehaus Museum, and the Chicago Cultural Center, pausing and performing small acts of neighborism at each venue, and end at SAIC Galleries with a gesture to mark the end of the exhibition Style is The Body Thinking. The public is invited to accompany the procession.
Leopold Benches: A P(o)or(t)ch Theater blends the retro technology of stereoscopic photography with live performance-based image-making and explores the porch as an emblem of generosity and social porousness at a moment of increasing isolation and division. Inspired by the writings of 20th-century conservationist Aldo Leopold, the work centers on a pair of benches designed to support attentive observation of the natural world. With a set of 12 original stereoscopic photographs guiding a two-hour score, the performance investigates how slight differences in perception can produce either heightened depth or clashing understandings of reality. The work was first performed at the 19th International Architecture Exhibition at the US Pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2025, and the Midwest Redux version was presented as part of Chicago Performs at the MCA in September 2026.
Poor Farm Experiment members include Michelle Grabner, Mark Jeffery, Kelly Kaczynski, Brad Killam, Kristin Mariani, and Judd Morrissey.
For more information on the project: https://mcachicago.org/whats-on/events/the-poor-farm-a-poortch-theater-midwest-redux/.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.

title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Guided Tour of the Newberry
description:
In 1893, the World’s Columbian Exposition took place in Chicago, Grover Cleveland started his second non-consecutive term as president, and the Newberry building opened to the public. On this guided tour, you’ll learn about the history behind the founding of the Newberry. You’ll also discover all the ways you can engage with the library today.
Founded in 1887, the Newberry had three temporary locations before moving into its permanent home across from Washington Square Park in 1893.
The library was designed by architect Henry Ives Cobb, with input from Newberry head librarian William Frederick Poole. Cobb envisioned a grand edifice on par with the civic landmarks of Europe; Poole favored a more modest design that would facilitate user access to books and other resources. In the end, they compromised. The Newberry is a blend of their competing visions.
Aerial photograph of the Newberry, 2022
Architectural detail on the Newberry's facade
The Newberry's Reference Reading Room
Over the years, the Newberry has grown and evolved, notably with the addition of a climate-controlled stacks building in the early 1980s and a renovation that updated spaces and restored original architectural details on the library’s first floor in 2018.
You’ll get a healthy dose of history on this tour. But you’ll also get to see the Newberry in action in the present. Tens of thousands of people visit the Newberry every year, and there are many ways that we make the library’s collections, programs, and resources accessible and relevant to them.
This tour is free, and no advance registration is required. We'll meet in the lobby of the Newberry and begin the tour from there.

title: Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? Gallery Hours
description:
Arts + Public Life at the University of Chicago presents Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? a new exhibition by Chicago artist Candace Hunter centered on the construction of the Dan Ryan Expressway and the Black communities displaced in its path. Now embedded within Chicago’s physical and social fabric, the Dan Ryan Expressway obscures both the choices that produced it and the lives reorganized around it. The construction disrupted the ordinary intimacies through which a place becomes home: routes traveled, neighbors known, businesses frequented, porches gathered on.
 Through photographic collage, architectural fragments, archival materials, sound, sculptural interventions, and oral histories, Hunter moves between what is documented and what is remembered. The work resists the idea that displacement can be understood solely through statistics.
 The series builds on the Memory Teas Candace hosted during her APL residency, which gathered first-person accounts from Black Chicagoans who remember the Dan Ryan’s construction and the neighborhoods transformed by it. Rather than asking these memories to complete the historical record, Hunter allows them to stay partial, layered, and unresolved.
 While centered on Chicago’s South Side, the history at the heart of Intentionality, 1960 reaches beyond the city. Across the United States, highway construction, redevelopment, and urban renewal reshaped Black communities, often presenting profound social and spatial disruption as necessary progress. Intentionality, 1960 invites audiences to see those histories not as isolated events but as part of a larger American story.
 Intentionality, 1960 will be accompanied by Threshold: Conversations on the Stoop, a series of public dialogues on the front porch within the exhibition between Candace and scholars to dive into topics related to the exhibition. The Threshold conversations are presented with support from the Office of the Provost Diversity and Inclusion team, in partnership with the Chicago Forum for Free Inquiry and Expression.
 Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? will be on view from September 24-December 12 in the Arts + Public Life Gallery Space located in the Arts Incubator at 301 E. Garfield Blvd.
 Gallery Hours: Thursday-Saturday | 1:00 - 5:00pm

address: 1 W University Pkwy, University Park, IL, 60484
description:
The Ruth Page Center for the Arts is proud to present its annual live production of “Ruth Page’s The Nutcracker” featuring original choreography by the legendary Ruth Page and directed by the artistic team: Victor Alexander, Birute Barodicaite, Dori Rothschild, Chrissy Lacny, John Atterberry and Renardo Johnson. 
Originally presented at the Arie Crown Theatre from 1965 until 1997, this production is Chicago’s longest-running Nutcracker tradition, recreating highlights from Ruth Page’s beloved original full-length staging. It features exquisite dancing, world-renowned guest artists, stunning costumes and magical settings in the Land of Snow and Kingdom of Sweets. International and local guest artists are featured alongside the talented dancers of the Ruth Page Professional Dance Training Program and students from Ruth Page School of Dance.   
Chicago’s longest-running “Nutcracker” has delighted tens of thousands of fans and the acclaimed full-length version comes to Governors State University’s Center for Performing Arts, 1 University Pkwy., Saturday, Dec. 5 at 2 p.m. and Sunday, Dec. 6 at 3 p.m. Tickets, ranging from $17 to $59 (depending on venue), are on sale now at RuthPage.org.

description:
Irish Christmas in America returns for its 21st season with a vibrant, family-friendly celebration of Ireland's Christmas traditions. The production brings together exceptional music, song, dance and storytelling in a performance filled with warmth, humor and festive energy.
Produced by Sligo fiddler Oisín Mac Diarmada, the 2026 company features Laura Jo on vocals and guitar; Gráinne Hambly on Irish harp and concertina; Caoimhín Ó Fearghaíl on uilleann pipes and flute; Samantha Harvey on piano and dance; and Jack Warnock on guitar and vocals. Evocative photographic images frame the performance, offering audiences a memorable glimpse into the history and spirit of an Irish Christmas.
First conceived in 2005, Irish Christmas in America was created to share traditional - and often little-known - Irish customs with audiences in the United States. Over two decades, the show has welcomed a distinguished roster of guest vocalists and established itself as a sparkling tradition on the holiday calendar.
“One of the most heartfelt themes of Irish Christmas is emigration,” says Mac Diarmada. “Music was a way that people stayed close to home.”

Steve Byrne has established himself as one of the most reliable and versatile stand up comedians working over the course of his 20 plus year career. Amongst the stand up community, he directed the acclaimed documentary on The Amazing Johnathan, "Always Amazing" which he is currently developing into a scripted television show. Most recently, Steve wrote and directed the semi autobiographical feature film about his early years in stand up comedy called "The Opening Act". Starring a roster of who's who in the stand up world (Bill Burr, Cedric the Entertainer, Russell Peters, Tom Segura, Whitney Cummings, Ken Jeong, Jimmy O Yang, Iliza and many others) the film was revered by stand up fans and critics alike sitting at 86% Fresh on Rotten Tomatoes.

title: Henry Fraser
description:
Henry Fraser performs Orexis, a new arrangement of his ongoing solo work made for Lampo. Beginning with the physical properties of the double bassits resonances, tactility, and scaleFraser explores the relationship between player and instrument, bringing the smallest details of the bass into focus: the sympathetic vibration of a string against a fingernail, the texture of fingers passing over a string, or beating patterns that emerge between tones.
Fraser draws on musical languages as disparate as Black American music, spectralism, Deep Listening, Gaelic psalm singing, and harsh noise. Rather than treating these as a succession of styles or techniques, he grounds them in a shared approach to the instrument, using microphones, EQ, and close listening to reveal layers within the sound.
Planned material and improvisation move through the same framework, with Fraser, as he puts it, collaborating with the bass and inviting the audience to listen its way into the music alongside him.
Henry Fraser (b.1991, Boston, Mass.) is a double bassist, composer, and improviser based in New York. His work centers on improvisation and collaboration and draws on a wide range of musical forms and practices. Since 2019, Fraser has focused intensively on solo music for the double bass, exploring resonance, physical gesture, and the acoustic properties of the instrument.
Collaborators include Ka Baird, John Zorn, Uniform, Mary Halvorson, Randall Dunn, and Joey Arias. Performances include Carnegie Hall and Lincoln Center, New York; National Concert Hall of Ireland, Dublin; and Unsound Festival, Kraków, among others. His latest solo album, Pneuma, was released by Kou Records in June 2026.
Fraser was an Art Omi Music Fellow in 2021 and a NYSCA/NYFA Artist Fellow finalist in Music/Sound in 2022. He held residencies at Pioneer Works and The Stone in 2025. Since 2023, he has worked as a teaching artist with Carnegie Halls Future Music Project, leading music workshops with incarcerated youth in New York City.

A 1930s Prohibition-era intrigue game about loyalty, power, and secrets, where every conversation could make or break an alliance.

Prohibition remains the law of the land, but the city drinks harder than ever, and gangsters fight tooth and nail to control the flow. The newspapers scream about shootings, the politicians make speeches about reform, and the real business happens after dark, under the table.
The speakeasy where you gather is more than a watering hole. It’s a crossroads where alliances are forged, secrets are traded, and debts come due. It’s neutral ground… at least until the guns come out.

There isn’t one single plot to follow; instead, there are webs of secrets, debts, romances, rivalries, and ambitions waiting for you to pull on them. You’ll decide what kind of story unfolds: vendettas, betrayals, power grabs, messy romances, or all of the above.

title: Rhye
description:
A mosaic of emotive piano keys, physical percussion, buzzing analog synths, and expansive vocals, RHYE find humanity in musicality. Shrouded in mystery, the group first surfaced setting the Internet abuzz with ambiguous imagery, sophisticatedly sensual music videos, and that distinctive falsetto. Following the runaway online success of two initial singles, the critically acclaimed debut album Woman (Loma Vista Recordings) was released in 2013 and lauded by critics from Pitchfork ("Best New Album") to The Guardian to New York Times.
Gifted songwriting, breathtaking vocals and deft instrumental arrangements combine to create an intoxicating blend of R&B influenced, deeply emotive music making the album a staple for provoking intimate moments.
Since the release of Woman, RHYE has relentlessly toured to establish a devoted global fanbase and enrapture crowds in theaters and at festivals worldwide including riveting sets at Coachella and Pitchfork Paris amongst many others.
Originally a duo conceived in the studio, RHYE has transformed into a collective led by vocalist and producer Milosh and elevated by a cast of accomplished multi-instrumentalists. As the band began writing new material, the expansive live show indelibly impacted the music for their second full-length album Blood, due for release February 2nd, 2018, resulting in a warmer, more organic sound. It's a new beginning and a new musical experience. It's RHYE.
