title: Syzygia
description:
Syzygia is a Chicago-based quartet that performs freely improvised music, bridging spontaneity with ideas and aesthetics from contemporary classical music. The group treats improvisation as extemporaneous composition, informed by the concepts, textures, and structures of 20th- and 21st-century classical music. Each member contributes a distinctive voice to the ensemble, shaped by their extensive histories in classical, jazz, and new/creative music.
Syzygia is Robbie Lynn Hunsinger - winds and strings, Jamie Kempkers - cello, Jeff Chan – flute and clarinets, and Michael Perkins – piano
$20 / $10 w/ Student ID - Tickets Available at the Door
Artist Bios
Robbie Lynn Hunsinger
Robbie Lynn Hunsinger is an interdisciplinary artist, composer, multi-instrumentalist and educator. She performs with Eastern and Western oboes, single reeds and fiddle often incorporating reactive visuals, micro-controlled motors and hacked game controllers. Her interactive art weaves original music and new media into playable environments using sculpture, projections, sensors and motors, creating frameworks for compelling sensory exploration. Conservatory trained as an oboist, she toured internationally as a classical and avant-garde instrumentalist with a career that includes concerts, tours and a Grammy with the Chicago Symphony and performances with the Atlanta Symphony, the Metropolitan Opera, Marlboro Music Festival, the Chicago Jazz Festival, FMP Festival, the Chicago World Music Festival and SXSW. She has played with Evan Parker, toured with Michael Vorfeld, studied with Roscoe Mitchell and her Trio album with Joseph Jarman and Tatsu Aoki received 4 stars from Downbeat Magazine. Her interactive installations have been written up in Make Magazine, supported by the NEA and exhibited at the MCA, ISEA and Thomas Blackman Gallery. This year she was selected to participate in the Chicago International Puppet Festival's Puppet Lab cohort and has active duet projects with Tatsu Aoki and Tim Daisy with soon to be released recordings. She is an environmental and animal activist and founded the Chicago Bird Collision Monitors. You can find out more about her @robbiehunsinger on FB & IG and at robbiehunsinger.com
Jamie Kempkers
Jamie Kempkers was a former student of classical cello repertoire who now finds creative fulfillment in improvisation and compositional experimentation in collaborative and solo work. He studied cello with Dr. Robert Ritsema and recorded with John Erskine at Hope College in Holland, Michigan. He has been living in Chicago, playing improvised and/or experimental music since 2001. Currently, he is a member of Tatsu Aoki's Miyumi Project and is also a frequent collaborator on the experimental dance projects of Yoshinojo Fujima. Jamie has just released a new album with Tatsu Aoki on Asian Improv Records, "The Amazing Music of Jamie Kempkers" https://www.asianimprovrecords.com/product-page/air119-d
Michael Perkins
Since the late 90s pianist/composer Michael Perkins has been regularly performing and recording in the punk, electronic, and jazz scenes in and around Chicago. He’s worked as a session musician on many recordings for bands like Atari Star, Das Kapital, and The Lavellas as well recording with his own groups such as Sig Transit Gloria, Written in the Sand, Far Rad, and Mr 666. Michael spent 7 years as a sound engineer working at various live venues throughout the city, and spent 3 years as the resident recording engineer for Harold Arts Artist Residency in south Eastern Ohio. After leaving Harold Arts, Michael and his partner Heather Lynn started Templehead Gallery, first in Humboldt Park and then later in Pilsen, and for 5 years provided a venue for young artists/musicians who were looking for their first solo art show. Since then, Michael has been continuing to play jazz and blues on a regular basis in addition to the occasional free improvised electronic music set.
Jeff Chan
Chicago multi-instrumentalist/composer Jeff Chan is committed to sharing the Asian American experience through music. With a discography of more than 20 recordings as a leader, sideman and producer, Chan has performed extensively in the Chicago area, across the nation and in Europe. Critics have said that Chan is “ a voice to be reckoned with (Brian Gilmore, JazzTimes)” and that his work is “music of uncommon majesty, spirituality and emotional depth (Howard Reich, Chicago Tribune).”

18-year-old Harrell "Young Rell" Davenport is a dexterous and inventive guitarist and a fat-toned harmonica phenom, Young Rell is already a commanding vocalist and a poetic and poignant songwriter. Whether he is accompanying himself on guitar while playing harmonica on a rack and singing, or alternating between guitar and harmonica with an ensemble, Young Rell sings his songs with sincerity and without a hint of affectation, working the stage with the poise and charisma of a veteran performer.
A prolific and engaging presence on social media, Young Rell has created a global community of fans and followers who have not only praised his talent but engaged enthusiastically with him on the subject of musicianship, musical instruments and past generations of famous and obscure blues inspirations.
As a child, Rell navigated personal struggles and trauma by immersing himself in music that was born in response to oppression and hardship. He found solace studying and expressing himself in the blues.
His community building and graceful social interaction have landed him relationships and experiences with the greatest blues artists alive today. He has been championed by Billy Branch, Kingfish Ingram, Bob Margolin, Bernard Allison and many others. title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.

Get more visitor information.

title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding.

Jenny Bienemann is a celebrated songwriter, poet and author whose work is a cornerstone of the Midwest folk community. Known for Haiku Milieu and her "Sunday church" routine exemplifying her ability to find the extraordinary in the everyday, Jenny’s music is a soulful blend of wit, wisdom, and acoustic elegance. Whether she is performing her own intricate compositions, performing with husband Robin or leading community-driven projects, her voice carries a warmth and clarity that feels both intimate and expansive.

Robin Bienemann is a renowned guitarist, songwriter and vocalist whose repertoire ranges from the sublime to strange new worlds. His wickedly funny and poignant original songs mix contemporary themes with old musical styles. He combines dry humor and sophisticated songwriting with a deep sense of history. At his musical core is a reverence for the guitar as an instrument to accompany songs and as a vessel to express the American psyche in all its strange beauty and complexity.
Robin revels in the delicious history of Chicago music. He combines Blues, Jazz, Country and Latin music with fingerstyle guitar to create a playground for his lyrical musings on science, animals and the whole scope of human experience. His songs are poetic, comical and educational. A flow of images ranging from vampires, insects, dinosaurs, dodo birds, work and romance.
Robin has shared the stage with Dan Hicks, Christine Lavin, Junior Brown, and Southern Culture on the Skids. He performs regularly solo, with his trio, and as a duo with Jenny Bienemann. Aikido (合気道) is a throwing and pinning art rooted in the same traditions as jiujitsu, but promotes a non-aggressive, non-competitive philosophy.
While many practice it for exercise or self-defense, its ultimate goals are the self-cultivation of a calm mind and relaxed body. Its lack of matches or contests (and the need to prepare for them) allows an inclusive environment in which students of varying age, skill and physical ability train together and side-by-side in a mutually supportive environment. An ideal option for the busy modern person seeking dynamic physical activity without hype or one-upmanship, or someone interested in martial arts but intimidated by more overtly combative styles. As the saying goes, pain is inevitable, suffering is optional. Most of us experience them as the same thing, but through meditation, mindfulness and the cultivation of self-compassion, we gain clarity into the power to heal ourselves.
 During this daylong retreat at the museum, Jon Aaron will guide meditation practices related to seeing, hearing, and working with pain and illness. All are welcome regardless of experience. In collaboration with Spiritual Life.
 Jon Aaron has been teaching mindfulness, meditation and Buddhadharma in the Insight tradition for over 25 years. He is a recent transplant from New York where he was a teacher at New York Insight Meditation Center and the Jewish Community Center of Manhattan. He is a founding member and current president of the Global Mindfulness Collaborative.

title: Writing the Past: Storytelling Workshop
location: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC), La Salle Banks Room
description:
Sunday December 6 and 13, 1:00pm–3:00pm, LaSalle Banks (basement) of ISAC.
 Instructor: Malayna Evans, PhD
 From character arcs and plot structures to processes and beat sheets, telling tales set in the ancient world requires more than enthusiasm. Join Malayna Evans, Ph.D., author of Neferura and Isis of Egypt for a hands-on workshop designed to guide writers through key aspects of crafting a manuscript. The coursework will touch on developing rich characters, creating plots with meaningful stakes, incorporating intentional themes into your work, drafting first lines that connect, establishing a strong point-of-view, finding an audience, and more. With a combination of lectures, discussions, and writing prompts, this two-week workshop will offer concrete tools and strategies for writers new to the craft as well as those who are seasoned.
 All registrants will receive a copy of Malayna’s latest book, Isis of Egypt: Goddess of Thrones is a feminist retelling about the woman behind one of the ancient world’s most widespread and enduring cults, a goddess whose message of empathy and resilience resonates still today.
 Malayna Evans earned her MAs in Greek and Roman history and the history of the ancient Near East and her Ph.D. in Egyptian history from the University of Chicago. She has written numerous books, including Neferura: The Pharaoh’s Daughter and the middle grade Jagger and Aria Jones series.

title: Live Performance, Film Screening & Discussion: Sweet Lorraine in Auschwitz
description:
Frank (Miša) Grunwald was just ten years old when the German invasion of Czechoslovakia upended his life. Torn from his family and imprisoned in five concentration camps, Frank found an unlikely source of solace and strength in American jazz. In the documentary Sweet Lorraine in Auschwitz, Grunwald, at age 89, retraces the places that shaped his story and reflects on endurance, loss, memory, and the music that helped sustain him through the Holocaust. Filmed across Europe at the sites central to his journey, the film offers an intimate portrait of survival and the enduring power of music amid unimaginable circumstances.
Join us for an afternoon of live music, film, and conversation. The program will feature a live performance curated by Chicago’s Emmy Award-winning trumpeter, composer, and educator Orbert Davis and his Jazz Quartet, bringing the music at the heart of Grunwald’s story into the Museum. Following the screening, Kelley Szany, Museum Senior Vice President of Education & Exhibitions and a featured scholar in the film, will moderate a discussion with director Philip Paluso, writer and producer Amber Maze, and co-producer Jamie Kramer about bringing Grunwald’s story to the screen and the intersections of testimony, history, memory, and music.
Free to the public. Reservation required.

title: They Are All Our Sons
address: 1333 N. Milwaukee Ave, 2nd Floor, Chicago, IL, 60622
description:
18+ ONLY
They Are All Our Sons is an immersive theatrical experience that reimagines one of our oldest myths, the Medusa myth, against the backdrop of a modern-day strip club. It's not just a play, but a tool for social change.
When two young dancers meet at the club, Athena quickly takes Medusa under her wing. The club encourages their bond, and soon they're sisters, dance partners, and the act everyone pays to see. But as Medusa grows obsessed with her own awakening, the power play between men and women, and finally healing from her past, she begins to challenge the stability of the only place Athena has ever felt in control.
The show moves through joy, resilience, pain, and rage, exploring the sisterhood wound and the systems of power the club operates within. We are left with the question: what if Medusa was never the monster? What if she was a woman who got labeled one because it was easier than holding a god accountable?

title: Durand Bernarr x Club1BD
description:
Erykah Badu. Kaytranada. Anderson .Paak. The Internet. Teedra Moses. They all have one thing in common—they’ve been blessed by the vocal brilliance and singular artistry of Durand Bernarr. 
The GRAMMY-nominated singer, songwriter, and creative force is redefining the landscape of progressive R&B. His presence in music is a masterclass in vocal dexterity, stage command, and fearless individuality. With a style that seamlessly fuses funk, soul, and avant-garde artistry, Durand has cemented himself as an artist without boundaries. 
Born in Cleveland, Ohio, Durand was immersed in music from a young age. Raised in a household where music was both a passion and a profession, his father, an audio engineer, and his mother, a vocal coach, exposed him to a wide range of sounds and techniques. By the age of 16, Durand’s innate talent had already led him to work as a production assistant for Earth, Wind & Fire, a formative experience that laid the foundation for his future career. His upbringing fostered a deep understanding of both the technical and emotional power of music, leading to a career that blends rich harmonies with innovative soundscapes. 
Durand first made waves in the early 2010s, gaining a cult following through his viral covers, which showcased his soaring range and unparalleled interpretative skills. His breakout moment arrived in 2016 with the release of Sound Check, a project that established his signature sound. Then came DUR& (2020), a critically acclaimed album featuring collaborations with Ari Lennox, Anna Wise, and Kaytranada, which solidified him as a creative powerhouse in the independent R&B space. 
Durand’s artistry has continued to evolve, with the release of Wanderlust and the GRAMMY-nominated En Route, which earned a nomination for Best Progressive R&B Album at the 67th Annual GRAMMY Awards. He also garnered a Grammy participation certificate for his feature on Kaytranada’s “Weird” from Timeless, which contributed to the album’s nomination for Best Dance/Electronic Album. His ability to cross genres and bring his distinct sound to various musical worlds has made him a force in modern R&B and electronic music. 
In 2023, Durand partnered with rising producer and songwriter duo Charlie Vettuno to release Charlie Vettuno PresentsWhere in the World is Carmen Randiego?!, an EP that marks the second creative pit stop between his sophomore album Wanderlust and the highly anticipated BLOOM. This collaboration highlights his continuous exploration of new sounds and collaborations, further pushing the boundaries of his musical identity. 
Durand’s live performances are nothing short of legendary. Whether gracing the stages of Afropunk, Bonnaroo, Essence Festival, or headlining his own Wanderlust Tour and Step Into My Office Tour, he brings a level of showmanship rarely seen in today’s industry. His electrifying Tiny Desk Concert in 2023 became an instant viral moment, while his work behind the scenes—co-directing and singing background vocals for Teedra Moses’s Tiny Desk performance—further displayed his multifaceted artistry. 
Now, with his highly anticipated third studio album BLOOM on the horizon, Durand is stepping into his most personal and intentional era yet. BLOOM is a heartfelt tribute to the love that exists beyond romance—the love found in friendship, self-discovery, and the communities that help us grow. “Through a fusion of music and personal reflection, I am honoring the bonds that have shaped my journey, the tribe that continuously pours into me, and the freedom to nurture spaces where love flourishes.” The album’s lead single, Impact, offers a glimpse into the emotional depth and sonic evolution of this next chapter. An artist’s artist, a showman’s showman, and a creative force that refuses to be boxed in—Durand Bernarr is here to stay.

title: Reclaiming the Choice: A Harm Reduction & Sober Curiosity Workshop for Adults
description:
A workshop for adults who are curious about their relationship to alcohol and other substances.
Maybe you’ve noticed the second drink showing up before you decided on it or maybe you’ve found yourself taking an edible without the desire. Maybe nothing feels “wrong,” exactly, and you’re just curious what life would feel like with a little less, or none, or something different. Our relationships with substances are rarely as simple as “problem” or “no problem.” Drinking and using often do something for us: they soothe, they cope, they connect, they celebrate, they quiet the noise. And sometimes substances end up taking away from the values we hold or the lives we want to live. In short, you might be asking: “Is this still working for me?”
In this gentle, supportive, and direct 2-hour online workshop, you’re invited to join Em, one of our behavioral therapists at Room to Breathe, to:
1. Explore your relationship with substances with curiosity rather than judgment: what substances provide, cost, and where urges might come from;
2. Learn about the neuroscience of reinforcement cycles and substance use;
3. Practice mindfulness and somatic skills to develop agency in your choices and values;
4. Be in community with others who are asking the same questions, without labels or verdicts.
What to expect: 
Psychoeducation on the continuum of use, what substances do for us, and the cycles that keep patterns going
Mindfulness and somatic practices to aid in reclaiming agency and choice
Practical, judgment-free harm reduction information and resources
Written and oral reflection, individually and in community
To protect participants’ privacy, only the teaching portions are recorded. All registrants get access to that recording for 30 days, plus a follow-up email with slides and additional resources.
This workshop is educational and is not a substitute for treatment or medical detox. If you drink or use heavily every day, please talk with a medical provider before stopping, as withdrawal can be dangerous.
Cost: Sliding scale pricing, $40-70; choose the amount that aligns with your financial situation. If this doesn’t feel financially feasible for you but would like to join the workshop, please reach out to Em directly to inquire about additional sliding scale options!

address: 10 S. Vail Ave., Arlington Heights, IL, 60005
description:
The Gaudete Brass is made up of five musicians who believe strongly in the expressive and communicative power of brass chamber music. Since 2004 the quintet has engaged in creatively expanding the brass quintet repertoire, developing unique programs that have resonated with chamber music audiences all over the country.
The group has engaged in live performances at venues such as Symphony Space and Merkin Hall in New York City and Millennium Park in Chicago, commissioned new works from noted composers such as Stacy Garrop, David Sampson, Jonathan Newman, Kile Smith, John Mackey, and Alice Jones, and appeared on radio broadcasts on WFMT in Chicago, WQXR in New York, and Nashville Public Radio. In the 2020-2021 season Gaudete received a grant from Chamber Music America for a series of online concerts broadcast live from our homes using the open source software Jacktrip.
Gaudete has also presented educational programs and concerts at prominent institutions including The Juilliard School and the Eastman School of Music, community outreach concerts for the Quad City Arts and the Virginia Arts Festival, and has enjoyed multi-year ensemble-in-residence positions at Carthage College and Roosevelt University’s Chicago College of Performing Arts.
While keeping this rigorous performance schedule, Gaudete has recorded four albums: Brass Outings (2006), winner of the CDBaby Editors’ Choice distinction and nominee for Just Plain Folks Best Classical Chamber Album; Conversations in Time with organist R. Benjamin Dobey (2011, Pro Organa); Chicago Moves, produced by Grammy winner Judith Sherman and featuring several of its commissioned works (2012, Cedille Records) and sevenfive (2017, Cedille Records) featuring five new works commissioned for Chicago’s John Corigliano 75th birthday festival.
Gaudete (gow-day-tay) is a form of the Latin word for “Joy.” We support the idea that chamber music, even (and perhaps especially) the serious kind, can powerfully communicate both the poignant and the exuberant.

Dr. Yulia Lipmanovich is a Russian-born concert pianist and distinguished piano educator based in Chicago. Trained in the distinguished Russian pianistic tradition, Dr. Lipmanovich is the Founder and Artistic Director of The Art of Piano Playing & Performing Arts, located in Chicago’s historic Fine Arts Building.
Dr. Lipmanovich began her musical studies at an early age with her mother, pianist and renowned teacher Madame Luba Lipmanovich-Yackobishvili, and later continued her studies in Moscow with the celebrated pianist Tatiana Nikolayeva. She received her Bachelor of Music degree in Piano Performance from The Juilliard School in New York, where she was a protege student on a full scholarship studied with the legendary pedagogue Madame Rosina Lhevinne. She earned her Master of Music degree from the Rubin Academy of Music at Tel Aviv University, studying with Professor Pnina Salzman and Professor Arie Vardi, and completed her Doctor of Musical Arts degree in Piano Performance at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where she studied with Professor Ian Hobson.
An award-winning pianist, Dr. Lipmanovich won the Soviet Composers Piano Competition in Moscow and the Young Artists International Competition in New York, leading to her debut recital at Carnegie Hall. Since then, she has appeared as a soloist with orchestras and in recital throughout the United States, Europe, Russia, Israel, and Asia.Her performances have taken her to many prestigious venues, including Carnegie Recital Hall, Alice Tully Hall, Steinway Hall, the Chicago Cultural Center, Studebaker Theater, and Ganz Hall at Roosevelt University. She has also performed throughout England, Italy, and Spain, including appearances at the Dartington International Summer School and the St. Lewis Music Festival in England.Among her notable Chicago performances are appearances on the Fazioli Concert Series, broadcast live on WFMT, and her acclaimed All-Russian Program at the Harold Washington Library Pritzker Auditorium, which was televised numerous times on WTTW.
She has also appeared at the Fine Arts Building Gala in Curtiss Hall, the Fourth Presbyterian Church Concert Series, and the Schubertiade at Pianoforte Chicago. As a concerto soloist, she has performed Grieg’s Piano Concerto in A Minor and Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1 with orchestra in Chicago.
Her performances have been featured on WFMT, WTTW, WGN, PBS, NBC, and FOX.
An inspiring and highly respected educator, Dr. Lipmanovich has served on the piano faculties of The Boston Conservatory, Boston College, Northeastern University, Daley College in Chicago, and the Rubin Conservatory of Music in Jerusalem. She currently serves on the faculty of the InterHarmony International Music Festival in Acqui Terme, Italy, and the Summit Music Festival in New York and Spain.In 2026, Dr. Lipmanovich began an artistic collaboration with the Conservatoire de la Vallée d’Aoste in Aosta, Italy, where she presented highly successful master classes for outstanding young pianists. She continues to be invited internationally to perform, teach master classes, and serve as an adjudicator for prestigious piano competitions.
Among her distinguished jury appointments, Dr. Lipmanovich served as an Honorary Judge for the Madame Rosina Lhevinne International Piano Competition in San Marco, Italy, as a juror for the Mozart International Piano Competition, and for the 5th Chopin International Piano Competition in Bangkok, Thailand, where she also presented solo recitals and master classes, including at Mahidol University, College of Music.
Dr. Lipmanovich is a member of the Music Teachers National Association (MTNA) and the Chicago Area Music Teachers Association (CAMTA) and is a Steinway Educational Partner.
As founder and Artistic Director of The Art of Piano Playing & Performing Arts, Dr. Lipmanovich is dedicated to developing the next generation of musicians through exceptional teaching, inspiring performances, and a lifelong commitment to artistic excellence. For more information, please visit: https://theartofpianoplaying.com
Alexander Tyfer is a violinist, conductor, composer, and educator whose career combines international performance, pedagogy, and musical research. Described by Mstislav Rostropovich as a “world-class violinist” distinguished by “versatile virtuosity, beautiful and expressive sound, artistry, and bright performing charisma,” Tyfer has performed as a soloist and chamber musician in the United States, Europe, and Russia.
He is a prize-winner of international violin and chamber music competitions in Russia, the United States, Italy, and Bulgaria.
Educated in the Russian violin tradition, Tyfer began his musical studies at the age of six. Since 1997, he has performed regularly as a soloist and conductor with orchestras in Russia, the United States, and Europe. He has served as concertmaster, soloist, and second conductor of the National Symphony Orchestra in Ufa, Russia, and as solo concertmaster of the Tchaikovsky Symphony Orchestra in St. Petersburg. In 2012, he toured extensively throughout the United States with the Tchaikovsky Symphony Orchestra, performing in New York, Chicago, Boston, Charleston, and other cities.
His repertoire encompasses major concertos and works by Vivaldi, Mozart, Paganini, Wieniawski, Mendelssohn, Bach, Beethoven, Brahms, Shostakovich, Khachaturian, Sarasate, Rachmaninoff, Kreisler, Tchaikovsky, Gershwin, and many others. He has also given first performances of works by contemporary composers who dedicated their compositions to him.
Tyfer has appeared at Carnegie Hall in New York and at international festivals in the United States and Europe, including the Peter the Great Festival in the Netherlands, New York Piano Festival, and Music Without Borders Festival in Portland, Maine. He has collaborated with distinguished musicians including Albert Markov, Alexander Markov, and Nina Beilina.

I’m M$ B’Havin Presents: “Not Your Typical Holiday Show”
I’m M$ B’Havin with my $exagenarian$:

Since April 1, 2026, I’m M$ B’Havin has had an Instagram following of over 82,000 and counting! On September 20, 2026, she offered her Instagram followers her first livestream performance at PianoForte Chicago, with an hour of Cabaret entertainment filled with adapted music by many great performers. Some of I’m M$ B’Havin’s favorite artists are: Lu Barker, Aretha Franklin, Buddy Guy, Screaming Jay Hawkins, Etta James, Vera Lee, Saffire-the Uppity Blues Women, Koko Taylor, Fats Waller, Steve Wonder.
On Sunday, December 6, 2026, by popular demand, she is offering her second one hour livestream show from 7:00 pm to 8:00 pm.
Originally from San Antonio, Texas, I’m M$ B’Havin moved to the Chicago area in the 1970’s. While in Chicago, she worked for two Fortune 500 companies, met her husband, Paul, and married him in Long Grove, IL. Eventually, she and her husband were transferred elsewhere. She became a mother of two and raised her children in the Detroit area. Eventually, her children moved to Chicago, and graduated from Chicago Columbia College. In 2012, I’m M$ B’Havin and her husband decided to relocate back to Chicago, which they now call home!
In 2015, she was diagnosed with Early Stage One Colon Cancer and had surgery to remove the cancerous tumor. A year later, her husband had heart surgery. They both begin to question their lives, their lost dreams, things they had set aside for their own careers.
In 2018, a friend suggested, they both start going to Buddy Guy’s Legends to listen to the Blues and dance. Paul started playing at Monday night Jams at Buddy Guy’s Legends.
In 2020, the pandemic hit. Music was the thread that held their family together! Soon, it hit I’m M$ $’Havin: a cancer diagnosis, her husband’s heart surgery! Time was flying off the shelf and it was time to rekindle her own lost dreams.
Once things began to feel normal again, she mentioned her singing idea to Buddy Guy! He said, “Once you start singing, don’t stop!” She stepped out of the shower and onto the stage on February 8, 2023, at the age of 72, and hasn’t looked back.
Over the past three years, she has performed in Chicago at Buddy Guy’s Legends, Fuller’s Irish Pub, The Tonk, Stars & Garters, the Marriott Naperville, and PianoForte. In October 2025, I’m M$ B’Havin and her husband, Paul went to Paris France with the Chicago Paris Cabaret Connexion to attend workshops and performed there.
Her band, the $exagenarian$, are named because of the age group of 69-69-year-olds! She chose the name because it sounded nasty. Her band consists of over 40 years of Blues Legend musicians, who have travelled and played in packed arenas on stages all over the world with well-known artists, such as, Buddy Guy, The Dells, Jerry Butler, Dionne Warwick, Aretha Franklin, and Pitbull to name only a few. Their music talent crosses into music genres of Blues, Jazz, Rhythm ‘n Blues, to Funk.
I’m M$ B’Havin says, “You can teach an old dog new tricks. Plus, I am living my best life as an evolving, captivating mature Cabaret Diva entertainer!”

title: Jamila Woods: 10 Years of HEAVN
description: Jamila Woods is a poet, singer, and multidisciplinary artist from the South Side of Chicago. Her critically acclaimed debut album HEAVN an ode to Blackness, girlhood, and home was released by JagJaguwar Records in 2017. Her sophomore project, LEGACY! LEGACY!, features twelve tracks named after writers, thinkers, and visual artists who have influenced the creators life and work including James Baldwin, Nikki Giovanni and Frida Kahlo. Her third album, Water Made Us (2023) is a genre-blending song cycle on love and the wisdom of surrender. The albums sequence is cleverly designed to echo the different stages of a relationship: the early days of easy compromising, flirtatiousness, and fun; the careful negotiation through moments of conflict or hurt; the grieving of something lost; and the tender realization at the end of it all that the person who is gone never really leaves, but stays with you as you find yourself ready to try again, refreshed and reassured. The albums sprawling 17 tracks span from autotuned RSend A Dove, to gentle acoustic folk rock on the heart wrenching Wolfsheep, to bubbly dream-pop on dance anthem Boomerang.Jamila has been featured on NPRs Tiny Desk, CBS This Morning, and The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. She has shared stages with Corinne Bailey Rae, Rafael Saadiq, Bonobo, Common, Chance the Rapper, Brittany Howard, Macklemore, and many others. In 2022 she served as artist-in-residence at the Clive Davis Institute of Recorded Music at New York University, teaching workshops on poetry, songwriting and live performance. An award-winning poet, Jamilas work often blurs boundaries between poem and song. As cultural critic Doreen St. Felix writes, It makes you wish all singers were poets.

title: Demetria Taylor Blues Band
description:
Demetria Taylor 
has been performing at BLUE CHICAGO 
since 2010. She is the seventh 
child of eight from the family of the late blues legend Eddie Taylor Sr. and is 
helping keep the legacy of her father alive.
Eddie is best known as the rhythm 
guitarist in the band of Jimmy Reed but he also had his own solo career and 
recorded some wonderful sides for the VJ label including the classic "Bad 
Boy". Her mother Vera Taylor was also a blues singer. Demetria has fond 
memories of blues greats and friends of the family coming by the house-- 
including Floyd Jones, Carey Bell, Sunnyland Slim, Johnny Littlejohn, Sam Lay, 
Willie Kent, Tail Dragger, Eddie Shaw, Johnny B. Moore and Magic Slim.
Born in Chicago, 
Demetria grew up surrounded by Blues music listening on records to her biggest 
influences including Etta James, Bessie Smith, Big Mama Thornton and most 
importantly, "The Queen of The Blues" Koko Taylor (no relation to the 
Eddie Taylor family).
Demetria started 
playing drums at age 14, coached by her older brothers Larry and Tim, both 
professional blues drummers. She played in family shows across Chicago which 
also featured brother Eddie Taylor Jr. on guitar. She also sang in the gospel 
choir at Trinity All Nations Church on Chicago's south side.
"I put God 
first and everything else will work out", says Demetria. "I feel that singing is something I was born to do. 
Sometimes on the stage my eyes tear up as I feel the music I'm singing. I love 
to listen to all types of music, but the blues caught my ear. I'll never give 
up my dream."
Demetria has 
toured nationally and internationally and performs in many clubs and festivals 
including the Chicago Blues Festival. Her first album, Bad Girl, is on Delmark 
Records. Demetria was nominated in 
2012 Blues Music Awards for 
"Best New Debut Artist".

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago

Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.

title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.

title: Pierre Bismuth: Love Bless America
location: Neubauer Collegium for Culture and Society
description:
This exhibition features new works by the French artist and filmmaker Pierre Bismuth. The centerpiece is a long-form meditative film documenting a creative collaboration between Joshua Abrams and Sharon Udoh, two leading figures from Chicago’s jazz and improvised music scene. Bismuth tasked them with composing a 21st-century spiritual based on a lyrical hymn he wrote for the project. The film traces the magic and workaday practice of “inspiration,” taking the traditions of religious music as a point of departure for a multi-layered reflection on love, music, and the divine. In addition to this new film, Bismuth will present a series of digital images resembling American flags emblazoned with lyrics from the hymn.
 Curated by Dieter Roelstraete.
 The Neubauer Collegium Gallery is free and open to the public. Gallery hours: M–F, 9–4.
 The Neubauer Collegium Gallery is supported by the Neubauer Family Foundation and the Brenda Mulmed Shapiro Fund. Additional support for this exhibition was provided by Bernard Friedman, the Helen Frankenthaler Foundation, and the France Chicago Center at the University of Chicago.

title: Anne Frank The Exhibition
location: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
address: 5700 S Lake Shore Drive, Chicago, IL, 60637
description:
ANNE FRANK: THE EXHIBITIONat Griffin MSI
Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding. 
Step inside the meticulously reconstructed Annex and reflect on the daily challenges, risks and courage of those who hid there before their arrest and deportation in 1944.
Anne Frank The Exhibition is a presentation of the Anne Frank House.

title: ISAC - Cultural Heritage Talk: 662 Missing Objects from the National Museum of Afghanistan
location: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC), Breasted Hall
description:
Join the Chicago Center for Cultural Heritage Preservation (C3HP), a center at the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC), for an afternoon talk:
 Missing from the National Museum of Afghanistan: 
 A New Database of 662 Lost Antiquities
 December 7th | 4:00 PM
 ISAC | Breasted Hall
 1155 East 58th Street, Chicago, IL 60637
 Talk and Q&A followed by a catered reception in the ISAC Director’s office. 
 Join us for a talk by Gil Stein, the director of the Chicago Center for Cultural Heritage Preservation (C3HP) and Rowe Professor of Near Eastern Archaeology at the University of Chicago, on C3HP’s newly launched database of posters representing 662 objects that are missing from the National Museum of Afghanistan.
 Between 2012 and 2021, the National Museum of Afghanistan (NMA) and the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC) engaged in a partnership that aimed to strengthen the NMA’s capacity to preserve the precious cultural heritage of Afghanistan and to facilitate an exchange of knowledge. From restoration work to digital documentation to training workshops to outreach programs to museum loss tracking, the partnership was multifaceted and succeeded in reaching its goals. One of the projects that came out of this partnership was the NMA Loss Assessment project, which confirmed that over 70% of the NMA’s collections had become unaccounted for, based on museum records predating the Afghan Civil War and the first period of Taliban rule. This enormous gap speaks to the devastating ravages of war that have plagued Afghanistan over successive decades, but it also speaks to the importance of the museum as an institution that preserves a people’s cultural heritage and collective identity through archival preservation and artifact conservation, in spite of the great personal risks that archivists and conservators face in doing so. To help recover these lost objects, C3HP has published a digital poster for each missing antiquity as an important new part of its recently launched website. Posting them online is meant to help museums, auction houses, art dealers, and law enforcement agencies recognize these objects as illicit antiquities: they should not be on sale, and they should be repatriated to the National Museum of Afghanistan. The digital posters, now available online at https://cultureheritage.center.uchicago.edu, aim to set the record unambiguously straight: these 662 missing antiquities rightfully belong to only one place, the National Museum of Afghanistan.
 To learn more about the National Museum of Afghanistan and the collaboration with ISAC that made this database of missing antiquities possible, please join us at 4 PM on December 7th in Breasted Hall at the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures. A catered reception will take place in the ISAC Director’s Office following the program. The talk will also be recorded and posted to C3HP’s YouTube channel at youtube.com/@c3hp. We hope to see you there! 
 **This event is free and open to the public. There is no registration.**

title: Matisyahu
location: North Shore Center for the Performing Arts
description:
Creativity is like a fire in a fireplace: You have to
tend it or it will go out. For nearly two decades, Matisyahu has kept his
creative spirit aflame by evolving his sound, melding genres, and testing the
limits of the musical traditions that have inspired him. His latest release,
Hold The Fire, and its leadoff single “Fireproof” takes inspiration from a fire
dream inspired by Matisyahu's Old Testament religion, which has meant so much
to his spiritual and creative life since his recording career began in 2004 and
his breakout track "King Without a Crown" blasted into the Billboard
charts in 2005. In a roundabout way, those same Old Testament roots
springboarded Matisyahu's music career.
Growing up outside New York City, the young Matthew
Miller followed jam bands like Phish and the Grateful Dead. Then, in Bob Marley
and reggae, he found that the messaging of Rastafarianism was sourced in part
from that same Old Testament. The sound that emerged on his first
albums—including his first two studio releases as well as 2005's Gold-certified
Live at Stubb's—embraced both the spirit of reggae and his spirituality and
roots in Judaism. Buoyed by hits like "King Without a Crown," albums
like the Grammy-nominated and Billboard No.1-ranked Youth in 2006, and the
Gold-certified 2009 antiwar hit "One Day" (streamed over 150 million
times on Spotify alone), he toured extensively through the second half of the
aughts with a high-energy stage show that has since grown to include more
improvisation. All the while his music expanded into a shapeshifting collision
of reggae, hip-hop, alt rock and boldly inventive pop. Today, he continues to
be inspired by evolving musical trends, finding linkages and loops between eras
and genres. Matisyahu's spirituality has evolved in parallel with his music,
though his Jewish heritage remains a central theme throughout his life and
music. The new EP, Hold The Fire (out February 2024), also finds him reflecting
on celebrity and artistic success. For Matisyahu, “the unbelievable and
miraculous feeling of being connected to our people” is what keeps the creative
fire alight.

title: The Imperfect City: Paul Goldberger
address: 111 E. Wacker Dr., Suite 1321, Chicago, IL, 60601
description:
Join us as we host the launch of Paul Goldberger’s new book, “The Imperfect City”, which explores how modern cities thrive when urban planning leaves room for happy accidents and innovations.
"The Imperfect City", by Paul Goldberger.
In "The Imperfect City", architecture critic Paul Goldberger explores what makes cities compelling: not the pursuit of perfect order, but the energy, beauty and unpredictability that shape urban life. Drawing on a lifetime of experiences in cities around the world, Goldberger examines how cities evolve through a combination of chance, accident and design.
Join Paul for a conversation with award-winning architecture critic Blair Kamin about the ideas behind "The Imperfect City" and what makes cities, including Chicago, so dynamic. Together, they’ll explore the role of architecture, design and planning in shaping the places we live.
Following the event, there will be a book signing of "The Imperfect City".
Paul Goldberger, a contributing editor at Vanity Fair, began his career at The New York Times, where he was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for distinguished criticism for his writing on architecture. Later, and for fifteen years, he was architecture critic for The New Yorker. He is the author of many books, including Building Art: The Life and Work of Frank Gehry, Why Architecture Matters, and most recently, Ballpark: Baseball in the American City. He teaches at the New School and lectures widely around the country on architecture, design, historic preservation, and cities. He lives in New York City.
Former Chicago Tribune architecture critic Blair Kamin is a winner of the Pulitzer Prize for criticism and numerous other awards, including the Order of Lincoln, Illinois’ highest civilian honor. Born in Red Bank, N.J., he is a graduate of Amherst College and the Yale School of Architecture. During a Nieman journalism fellowship at Harvard during the 2012-13 academic year, Kamin became fascinated by the 25 gates that enclose Harvard Yard and co-taught a class about them during Harvard’s January term. The eight-day class led to a thirteen-year journey that has culminated in a new clothbound edition of the widely-praised guidebook “Gates of Harvard Yard.” Previously issued in paperback, the book reveals the beauty, history, lore and legacy of Harvard’s often-overlooked sentries. Kamin edited the book, which is published by Harvard University Press and includes a foreword by Pulitzer winner Ann Marie Lipinski, formerly editor of the Chicago Tribune and curator of Harvard’s Nieman Foundation for Journalism.

ODD NIGHT OUT: A Benefit Show for the Orange Tent Project at Subterranean on December 7
Since 1994, Subterranean has been a cornerstone of the Wicker Park live music & nightlife scene. Built in the 1890s, the historic structure at 2011 W North Avenue has a storied past, having once served as a brothel, a bathhouse, and as a wire room for gambling during the prohibition era. Owner Robert Gomez has worked hard to preserve the original features of the space that have been in place since the building’s creation and give Subterranean its one of a kind character, including the iconic Tiffany & brass chandelier that hangs above the dance floor. The Subterranean stage has played host to notable and legendary acts including Chappell Roan, Turnstile, Dinosaur Jr, Lizzo, Tame Impala, Charles Bradley & His Extraordinaires, Halsey, Pussy Riot, Built To Spill, Brand New, BADBADNOTGOOD, Lee Scratch Perry, Alabama Shakes, Durand Jones & The Indications, Fall Out Boy, and has been home to some of Chicago’s longest running residencies: Thursday nights’ Reggae Gold and the longest-running hip-hop open mic in the nation, the 606 Open Mic.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.

title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.
